subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   BUSINESS OF SUPPLY FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GRANT ALLOTTED DAY
MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   BUSINESS OF SUPPLY FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GRANT ALLOTTED DAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move a motion for the adjournment of the House, for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration and falling within the responsibilities of the government under the heading of supply, as admitted by the President of the Privy Council, namely, the refusal of the government to grant an allotted day within the provisions of Standing Order 58.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   BUSINESS OF SUPPLY FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GRANT ALLOTTED DAY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has given the Chair the required notice under the provisions of Standing Order 26. This has given the Chair an opportunity to reflect on the important point raised by the hon. member. In passing, may I thank the hon. member for the background documents submitted by instalments to the Chair, which have been found both interesting and intellectually stimulating.
As all hon. members know, Standing Order 58 is the governing order in relation to the matter raised by the hon. member for Peace River and deals, generally speaking, with the businesses of supply and ways and means. Under that Standing Order, at the commencement of each session, there is designated by motion a continuing order of the day. The parliamentary timetable for the consideration of business under Standing Order 56 is divided into three distinct periods. One of these periods terminates not later than December 10, and during that time five sitting days shall be allotted to the business of supply. The second period of the timetable expires not later than March 26 of each year, and during that time a further seven days is allotted. This brings us to the third distinct period, which ends not later than June 30. In each of the periods, and more particularly for the purposes of the current problem, two days may, at the option of members in opposition, be declared to be non-confidence days.
The question the Chair has to determine is whether or not, during the period commencing March 27 and expiring on June 30, that the hon. member refers to as "the refusal of the government to grant an allotted day" is the foundation for an adjournment debate under Standing Order 26. The requirements of Standing Order 26 are well known to all hon. members. Section 5 of the Standing Order states that in determining whether a matter should have urgent consideration Mr. Speaker "shall have regard to the extent to which it concerns the administrative responsibilities of the government or could come within the scope of ministerial action-"
Precedents extending over a long period of time indicate that these words always have been interpreted as referring to a sudden emergency requiring immediate ministerial intervention. The Standing Order has never been interpreted as applying to the operation of other Standing Orders. In this particular instance, the hon. member's proposed motion seeks precisely to adjourn the House for the purpose of discussing the operation of Standing Order
April 16, 1974

58, a situation which in my view is not contemplated by subsection (5) of Standing Order 26.
In the circumstances, I am afraid I cannot agree with the contention of the hon. member for Peace River that an adjournment debate under the provisions of Standing Order 26 can be invoked to debate the application or the interpretation of another Standing Order.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. It concerns a very dangerous practice that seems to be creeping into our proceedings. In the absence of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) yesterday, a very important study which had been commissioned by the Canadian Consumer Council was released by the minister's office. The study deals with the consumer interest in regulatory boards and agencies. It has been in the minister's hands since June. We understand the minister has every right to have this document as long as it is necessary for him to understand it. We further understand it takes the minister a little longer than most to be able to absorb what is in these documents.
My point of order is that this document more properly should have been placed before the House under the provisions of Standing Order 41. I raise this point to get the guidance of Your Honour, because if parliament is sitting and if ministers are allowed to circumvent the rules in this way, I see no purpose in parliament being in session in the first instance. This very important document should be officially laid on the table of the House under Standing Order 41. I say the minister is in contempt of this House by circumventing the rules and releasing this study outside the House yesterday.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   BUSINESS OF SUPPLY FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GRANT ALLOTTED DAY
speechtext:
I am not sure that the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) requires a ruling of the Chair. He has raised a point of order. There being no further debate, I wonder whether it would be helpful for the Chair to make a ruling.
This standing order clearly provides a way for ministers of the Crown to table documents. It was introduced several years ago in order to make it easier for members of the ministry to table documents without points of order and without debate. I am not sure the standing order can be interpreted as imposing an obligation on ministers to table documents in the House under Standing Order 41. That may be so, although I do not think I could interpret the standing order as it now stands in that way.
It may well be that the standing order was designed and devised to make it possible for ministers to table their documents, and to encourage them to table them in the
Oral Questions
House rather than publish them outside the House. My impression is this general rule has been followed for some time. I have not observed, nor have I sought to observe or study, whether there has been a departure from that rule. I will perhaps look at the matter in this light. However, my ruling on the point of order raised by the hon. member will have to be that I cannot interpret the standing order as imposing an obligation on the minister to table the document or to publicize the document under the terms of Standing Order 41.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, April 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-14, to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, be read the third time and do pass, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Howard.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before ten o'clock last night I had been pointing out that it is difficult for the small businessman to accumulate capital. Capital accumulated in a farm or business has often been used for purposes of a retirement pension for the owner and his wife. The advent of the basic old age pension, the Canada Pension Plan and the provision for increasing the size of these pensions in accordance with the increase in the cost of living has made the accumulation of an annuity for use after the normal retirement age of 65 almost superfluous. Certainly it is less important. No

amount of saving which the normal person is able to do can match what the government has offered by indexing the cost of living as it applies to the basic old age pension and the Canada Pension Plan. Therefore, the accumulation of capital to be used as retirement income is much less important now than it was even four or five years ago. Indeed, one could enter one's retirement years in a shroud, so to speak, and still be assured of a fairly reasonable living because of state help.
What I am saying is that we are entering a new era in which there are new attitudes toward accumulation of capital. People think differently about savings. This, of course, has a great deal to do with the legislation before us. Today, five of the major banks set their prime lending rate at 10.5 per cent following the move of the central bank. They did this to stimulate savings because at present inflation rates one can borrow money virtually at zero cost: the rate of inflation is greater than the rate of interest. One would be foolish not to borrow money under such circumstances.
In today's Globe and Mail appears an article by a member of the C.D. Howe Research Institute. The author points out that our savings will supply insufficient capital for our needs in the 1970s and 1980s. That fact will affect the workings of this legislation. Will our financial institutions have enough funds to make this bill effective? Furthermore, the article points out that a high proportion of people in the 20 to 35-year age group save relatively little of their income. This proportion will remain high for the next decade. The author makes one assumption which I feel is not likely to be fulfilled. He assumes that with rising personal incomes people will save more. The evidence does not bear him out because as the state, by paying the Canada pension and the basic old age pension, will look after people in their retirement years, it seems evident that savings will not be that important.
This bill will not do much to help the small businessman in the short term. The sharp increase in the Bank of Canada lending rate has come about in response to the increase in the number of bank loans. The banks evidently were running out of money to lend. It is difficult to say who was getting these loans. It appears that some of this money was used for purposes of liquidity. Apparently it has not been lent to those whom this legislation is supposed to help.
That brings me to this point: business has not been able to expand in the last few years and now we are paying the penalty by seeing shortage of supply and lack of capacity for the production of goods. The minister suggested shortly after introducing the bill that losses in connection with farm improvement loans have been remarkably low, amounting to about one-fifth of one per cent of the face value of loans. That may be so. The significant fact is that we are facing a real shortage of supply of agricultural products, which indicates that the loan program has been administered too rigidly.
One of the prime causes of inflation is the steadily expanding tendency of governments to spend more and more of the gross national product. The increase in the bank rate of interest is designed to cut down consumer demand and is a modest effort to moderate the increase in the money supply. That brings me to this point: this bill
April 16, 1974

will not be effective unless money can be directed, through the medium of small loans, to farmers, fishermen and small businessmen. A good deal of it will be lent by the banks. To keep costs down, the government should reduce the increase in its rate of spending.
Most government spending is inflationary because it consists of transfer payments which are spent immediately. Savings could be redirected through such institutions as the Industrial Development Bank which could be told to take greater risks with small loans so that small businessmen have access to capital. The administration of these loans acts could take greater risks in order to aid small businessmen, farmers and fishermen. I have some serious doubts whether raising the ceiling on these loans will be as beneficial as it should be unless certain directions are taken in lending money to individuals, farmers in particular. Unfortunately, governments federal and provincial become so involved in lending money to the agricultural industry that not much private money is left for investing. In other words, we look to this type of legislation for much of our total investment in farming.
As far as farming is concerned, we are in general agreement that the family farm is one of the best units for agricultural production and for the fabric of our rural countryside. When one considers that in the Soviet Union the state is considering extending farm units so there will be emerging many larger farms, we might ponder the philosophy of enlarging farm units even more. I reject the point of view that we need abnormally large farm units. However, we must recognize that in this country, and particularly in the farmlands of western Canada, very large acreages are being farmed as units with a minimum number of families involved. Much of the reason for these large-sized units has been the availability of government-financed loans obtained by individuals who would not have been able to expand had they had to depend on private money. In other words, governments both federal and provincial have made possible larger units than the private lending institutions would have allowed.
In this bill which extends the loan limits we have the elements of an undesirable feature, and this will be used by owners of large farms to acquire even larger units. If these loans could be earmarked for individuals with smaller operations, it would help them become more self-sufficient and more viable. At the same time, it would ensure that large-scale operators would have to acquire their money from private lending institutions for any expansion they wish to undertake. This is preferable to the suggestion that farm sizes should be limited by legislation.
Farm improvement loans might well have the social function of preserving small farms and assisting new and young farmers to become established. They might well have to assume more risks than those in which the lending institutions are currently involved. Farm population has dropped from almost 40 per cent at the beginning of World War II to 7 or 8 per cent at the present time. Many people consider this abnormally low. With the worsening energy shortage it is evident that more individuals will have to become involved in food production. Indeed, a great deal of food has always been produced by units which were
Loans Acts Amendments
considered by the so-called agricultural experts to be inefficient.
We have to realize that the term "viable unit" has many different aspects and means many different things within an individual's life. I think the banks which are involved in the loan operation under this legislation could take more risks and give small and new operators more risk capital. The aspect of the bill which raises the limits will not let the operator become more viable or the new operator become established unless direction is given to lending institutions that these people should have a preferred position.
Turning to small business, this is an area in which I am very interested. I sincerely believe that small business provides a very strong pivot in our economy. It provides a built-in flexibility that large corporations cannot match. While it may not always be efficient, enough of it is efficient to make it an extremely valuable component of our society. In addition to the lending aspect or liability of small business, the most important thing for small business is that government leaves them alone. They are deluged with inspectors and advisers who create work and are an unnecessary expense for government. This is a much greater problem for small businesses than that of raising money. In fact, if governments could limit their demands on the management of small business it would go a long way toward making small business more viable. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me the opportunity to speak on this bill.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I again rise to speak on Bill C-14 because of great personal concern and obligation to many of my constituents, namely, small businessmen and their allied suppliers. When I spoke during the second reading debate on this bill last Wednesday I had the impression there would be an opportunity to move an amendment. Because we receive limited warning as to when a bill will be brought before the House I expected to have that opportunity when the bill was at the standing committee stage. However, immediately following second reading the House went into committee of the whole which, according to my limited knowledge of parliamentary procedure, did not allow for amendments.
The content of the amendment I would have moved would have counteracted what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said was not in the bill when answering a question put to him by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) in committee of the whole. I quote from page 1396 of Hansard:
I have a further question, Mr. Chairman, with regard to the small business loans. Is this going to allow for the operation of the business, or is it strictly for the purchase of property and machinery?
The minister replied:
It is not for working capital, Mr. Chairman.
Having experienced first-hand the need for such working capital in my own business in the early stages of its existence, I feel very strongly that the minister, along with the amendments that were included in the bill, should have given very serious consideration to a provision for working capital. Perhaps it is quite easy for the Department of Finance to overlook the importance of and the necessity for working capital. The minister and his
1466

April 16, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
department are so accustomed to being big spenders that they cannot comprehend the plight of small business owners. They obviously do not appreciate the fact that the only way many small business owners can survive is to take out only enough money after meeting employee payroll and operating expenses to provide the bare essentials for their families.
The absence of working capital is not nearly as evident in the two segments of the bill dealing into the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. These two areas are not involved in having accounts receivable to contend with to the same extent as the small businessman. As I have stated before, the most crucial area that has contributed to the bankruptcy of small businesses has been the lack of working capital. The business is launched, in many cases, with very little surplus cash in the bank. In many cases, if the owner could trade the overabundance of enthusiasm he must have possessed in order to have had the nerve to start the enterprise in the first place, for some working capital he would not have too many financial problems as he progressed. However, this is not the case, as the minister indicated. The bank demands sufficient collateral before lending small business any money. This in essence proves, even if the loan is granted, just how necessary it was in the first place.
Mr. Speaker, the necessity for freer working capital has always seemed so evident that I cannot help but wonder why it has not exercised a more important influence in the structuring of this bill and similar bills over the years since the introduction of the act. The most obvious reason working capital is not considered is that receivables have not nearly the collateral value of physical structures, equipment or real estate. However, take away receivables and most business would not need to exist. So they are, Mr. Speaker, an important cog in the cycle of success. But for banks to use this excuse to support their negative approach to small business loans only supports my further argument that banks should have some degree of obligation to make loans supported by applications which obviously if approved would help the advancement of Canadian products and also create more employment.
We have ambitious young people and, yes, some not so young who, given financial encouragement beyond the normal guidelines laid down for lending money, would continue to create the ideas necessary to keep alive the free enterprise system which has been so significant in our first century of Canadian progress. I have many constituents who are interested in starting a business or looking for ways to continue one already in progress. But by the time they have checked the sources of capital and the red tape involved, they are either discouraged from pursuing their dream of a business of their own or ready to throw up their hands in frustration at being able to continue the one they already have.
Mr. Speaker, we spend a lot of time debating how to encourage more Canadian investment. One obvious way would be to encourage the banks to show some compassion to our small business community, thus discouraging them from having eventually to sell out to foreign investors in order to keep from ultimate bankruptcy. But the only way

I can see banks ever doing this is to make it obligatory for them to loan to at least a percentage of applicants. The minister in committee of the whole stated as follows:
I suppose the best way to know what is going on in terms of refused applications is for members, when they are approached by their constituents regarding refused loans, to inform me of these complaints and I will make inquiries directly from the bank concerned to find out what the reasons were for the refusal. I am prepared to do that on a continuing basis.
To me, Mr. Speaker, that sounds like a very diplomatic way of passing the buck, and as far as I am concerned the taxpayer sees far too much evidence of buck-passing now. There must be guidelines laid down so that the banks and their potential customers know what could take place. I do not blame the banks for not wanting to be any more involved than is necessary, and past lending statistics will bear this out. The fact is that from the date the Small Businesses Loans Act came into effect in January, 1961, until September, 1973, approximately $283 million was lent for all of Canada. This is about $23 million per year on average. But something is wrong when we find the loans total for small business was no more in 1973 than in 1972, being about $15 million per year. And now Mr. Speaker, with the recent turn of events of the central bank's interest rate increasing, we will probably see less activity than before. Not only will we see growth restriction, but small business owners already in a bind for working capital will find increased costs in maintaining inventory and receivables because of an interest rate of probably 12 per cent.
Many businesses in the past have had to resort to shortterm loans of 12 per cent, or even much higher, from private sources but now they will be faced with 12 per cent from even the banks, and heaven knows how high from private sources. I am afraid this could be the so-called straw that broke the camel's back. Mr. Speaker, many very credible businesses have already exhausted their credit supply. There have been many legitimate reasons for this increase in the cost of doing business. If they are retailers, an increase in the price of the merchandise they sell means more inventory cost. If they are small manufacturers, the increased cost of maintaining inventory also applies. In both cases their cost of maintaining higher receivables will increase.
No one denies business today is strong, and all types of small business is no exception; but with runaway inflation so evident in every phase of our economy, many small businesses could be unknowingly accelerating themselves right into bankruptcy. Unhappily, the government has proven itself bankrupt of any solutions which might slow down this inflation. The inflation we see all around us is not totally induced from outside, as this government would have the Canadian people believe. Better than half of the now well over 10 per cent total inflation rate could be slowed down by a responsible government. It is obvious that we cannot expect any new ideas for fighting inflation from this government, but for the sake of Canada's future let us hope we shall not have to wait too long before the Canadian people have the opportunity to change the government.
As was stated earlier by my colleague from Ottawa West (Mr. Reilly) 60 per cent of the labour force in Canada is supported by small or medium-sized business. That statement in itself should be encouragement to take another
April 16, 1974

hard look at just how little these amendments will actually do for small business. Mr. Speaker, couple that statement with the fact that even though actual farmers represent only 5 per cent of Canadians, when you include all segments of our economy allied to agriculture the figure is raised to 70 per cent. This government is looking over or, perhaps I should be saying, overlooking a lot of people who I am afraid have been taking too much for granted.
However, Mr. Speaker, I realize it is too late at this stage to do any more than remind the architects of this bill, whoever they may be, of some of its shortcomings. The real changes will have to wait until the citizens of Canada have the opportunity to vote out of office this government which seems determined to stay in power even though their incompetence is becoming more and more evident week by week.

subtopic: FARM IMPROVEMENT, SMALL BUSINESSES AND FISHERIES IMPROVEMENT LOANS ACTS AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LOANS AND GOVERNMENT LIABILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of participating in the debate on Bill C-14. Although in past years I had the opportunity of serving on the Standing Committee on Fisheries, changes in the electoral boundaries removed from my riding practically all the area in which fishing was an important matter of concern. The result is that at the present time I am inclined to leave discussion of the fisheries aspect to my hon. friends whose constituents are more concerned with that industry.
Nevertheless, in case there should be some misunderstanding, I want to state emphatically that I still have a strong interest in the fishing industry. When we remember the part the Fraser River system plays in maintaining these resources, it is understandable that such an interest should continue. However, it is my desire today to comment on the provisions of the bill which relate to agriculture, an industry of major proportions and consequence in my riding. I should like to deal, too, with the aspects of the bill which affect small businesses of which there are a great many in Fraser Valley East.
When I spoke on the budget last year, I stated that small business in Canada generates more employment, real growth, tax revenue, and bears more of the cost burden of government than does so-called big business. Small businesses are the backbone of the Canadian business community. For as my colleague from Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) pointed out the other day, they create over 50 per cent of the nation's gross national product and pay close to 50 per cent of the taxes collected by the government, while employing more than 50 per cent-I think the suggestion has even been 60 per cent-of the people working in Canada.
Canada, as was the case with most developed countries, had as its dominant form of enterprise before World War II, small business. I do not mean that there were no large corporations before that, but I do mean that the bulk of all manufacturing and trade was in the hands of family business and regional organizations. In 1951 the dominion bureau of statistics showed that 90 per cent of all retail stores, service establishments, wholesalers and manufacturers had less than 15 employees and accounted for over 30 per cent of the gross national expenditure.
Loans Acts Amendments
Moving to the present day, Mr. Speaker, much of the output of our farms and factories is distributed to consumers through wholesale and independent retail stores. Many people who have studied economics have pointed out that the destruction of the small merchant carries with it a number of unfortunate and undesirable consequences, such as a depression in real estate values of business properties, a decline in tax revenues to municipalities, a complete displacement of normal credit arrangements within the community, and increased unemployment.
As well I should like to quote a former minister of the Crown, the Hon. E. Davie Fulton. Speaking in the House on May 30, 1960, as reported at page 4341 of Hansard, he said:
-the best and soundest economy is that economy which is based upon the maximum participation of the greatest possible number of independent operators in that economy, and that it is an unsound economy which relies for its operations either on the employment of everybody by the government or the employment of everybody by some giant corporation or corporations. Our objective, therefore, and our philosophy in this field is to bring the maximum reconciliation in the way of the protection of small businessmen, on the one hand, and the interests of the community, of the consumers and of society generally, on the other.
That is still the philosophy of this party when it comes to small business. This bill shows the government is taking a step in the right direction, however, in raising the gross revenue allowable portion from $500,000 to $1 million and the amount of the loan from $25,000 to $50,000. As I say, this is a step, but I am sure the government has come to grips with the real problem. Small business in Canada is fighting for its very survival.
Part of the problem is that all businesses are valued either by the federal government from the point of view of assessing capital gains, or by provincial governments for estate tax purposes, either on the basis of seven times the profits or the net assets value, whichever is higher. Both levels of government assess the small business as though it were a pile of cash in the bank or on the desk from which each can take its shares, and possibly more than its share. It is wrong, I feel, to look on small business in this manner. It is not a pile of cash on the table; it is a vital, dynamic enterprise and should be treated as such. We must ensure that conditions remain favourable for small business to grow and thrive. This can be done through stimulative and expansionary tax regulations.
There have been many instances in which the taxes have been so onerous and the available funds so scant that small businesses have had to be sold in order to satisfy the tax collector. Because of this, those who have been the proud owners of businesses that have been in the family for generations are forced to sell out and compete on an inadequate labour market. It is my position, and the position of this party, that provision should be made for Canadian citizens to invest in the equity of Canadian-owned small business. We believe that the credit, which will be 50 per cent of qualified investments to a maximum of $5,000 each year, should either be offset against the person's income tax or rebated directly to him. This means that a Canadian who invests, for example, $1,000 in a qualified business or company will receive a credit of $500 against his income.
1468

April 16, 1974
Loans Acts Amendments
Another matter of great concern to the small businessman is the proliferation of duties imposed upon him by government, for which there is no compensation. The records dealing with unemployment insurance, taxes, workmen's compensation and statistical data of various kinds require hours of additional work per week and, of course, these many additional hours of work must of necessity be compensated for in higher prices for the goods and services provided. This is a matter that is constantly being raised by constituents engaged in small businesses who cannot see any adequate justification for many of the records they are required to maintain. As an aside, one constituent discussed with me the seemingly ridiculous demand made upon him by an income tax official who, in spite of the fact that his income tax forms had been filed and the auditors had been out to check his books and records and had confirmed their accuracy, warned him against destroying the files as he must store them indefinitely in case they wished to audit them again at some time in the future.
There are a multitude of demands and restrictions which, taken individually, are seemingly insignificant but which when accumulated make the small businessman wonder whether it is worth the trouble to remain in business. The small businessman provides a personalized service to the community in the conduct of his business as well as in his participation in community projects and activities. On the other hand, the large supermarket complex tends to be impersonal and perhaps aloof from community activities. In many instances the small business is found in areas where the population is of lower density than large urban communities, but here as well the small businessman provides a service that is worth preserving. The small businesses of our nation are operated by individuals who are not expecting to become giants in business or multimillionaires, but who desire to provide for themselves and their families a decent and respectable standard of living while contributing to the social, cultural and economic life of the community.
The small businessman is faced with another serious problem today, and that is how to cope with the results of the inflationary spiral in the matter of help. Many have stated their inability to obtain help even in areas of high unemployment. The rejoinder to that may well be that if a business cannot afford to hire help at the going rate, the owner had better shut up shop. But the question is, what is going to happen if thousands more do close up shop and go on to the labour market? Not only will we have the unemployment picture aggravated; we will have a great many intensely independent, public spirited individuals who are disillusioned and bitter over the fact that government action, or inaction, has forced them to close their doors.
In the Speech from the Throne the government promised counselling services as well as financial assistance for small business, but I am not convinced that the measures proposed will solve the problems faced by small businessmen. This will require much more adequate and far reaching measures. However, this bill may assist them in meeting for the moment the crisis of inflation, taxation, and a completely unnecessary and burdensome maze of red tape so far as their efforts to be responsible and worthy members of society are concerned.

I shall now proceed to another subject, although I would have liked to continue on the matter of small businesses. Let me refer to the bill as it relates to the agricultural industry. Canadians in this category are seemingly a vanishing breed. As pointed out in the National Farmers' Union submission to the government of Canada on March 14, 1973, the census statistics of 1971 indicate that Canada suffered a net loss in the number of farms of 64,394 from the census figures of 1966. This was considerably higher than the previous five-year period of 1961 to 1966 when the number of farms decreased by something over 50,000. In fact, it is about a 28 per cent increase.
These figures must be saying something to us; they must be telling us that in spite of the shortage of jobs on the labour market, thousands of Canadians are finding it impossible to overcome the obstacles in the path of continuing to maintain and operate a farm. Cost of land and equipment is such that ever-increasing amounts of capital are required and the returns are not sufficient to justify the risk of expansion at the current cost of money obtained on the open market. The provisions of Bill C-14 as they relate to agriculture are welcome, but in light of present developments it is questionable if even the expanded credit facilities proposed will meet the needs of today. As has been pointed out in this debate, it is questionable if even $100,000 is sufficient to establish a viable working agricultural unit.
The point has been raised that legislation providing for increased credit will be of little value if lending agencies can find a more lucrative investment in other areas requiring capital. I think sufficient illustrations have been given us during this debate to indicate that this is not a hypothetical situation, and it is possible that a very careful monitoring program will be required to ensure that what has been done theoretically by law will in fact become a practical program as far as the farming community is concerned.
I would just say in conclusion that while welcoming the amendments which are before us today, and without questioning the fact that they will assist these various areas of our economy to a degree, they fall far short of meeting the needs in the areas of fisheries, small business and agriculture today.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to continue with the views so well expressed by the previous speaker, recognizing that in relation to the scope of this bill it is a shame a debate has to be undertaken by this House at all, since it provides the small business community and the small farming and fishing communities with so little. Indeed, considering the time devoted to this bill, it might well be said that never have so many words been said to accomplish so little for so few. Yet it is justifiable that the House deal with this bill in view of the significance of the issue. The significance of small business and the farming and fishing communities to the well-being of Canada as we have known it and would like to know it in the future cannot be overestimated. It is fundamental to the character of the Canada we have known and prized that the individual should have an
April 16, 1974

opportunity of entering into a business supporting himself and providing work for others.
The fact is that Canada needs leadership to preserve that tradition, and the present government, particularly with NDP support, is veering away from it. Canada is on its way to becoming a corporate and collective state in which the vast majority of people make their living in the employ either of big corporations or of big governments. One of the things this debate on the small business, farm and fisheries loans bill indicates to me and to the country is that we must try to recover the opportunity Canadians have traditionally enjoyed of entering enterprises on their own, of supporting the family farm and those participating in the important fisheries industry.
I think it is significant, when we look at statistics on income received by Canadians over the past 12 years, to note that the percentage of the national income enjoyed by small businesses has fallen from 10.4 per cent to 7.5 per cent, while at the same time the income for corporations has increased from 13.8 per cent to 16.3 per cent, with the income of governments increasing even more. At this time, governments in Canada at the three levels combined represent almost 40 per cent of our gross national product. Between governments and corporations well over half the income of this country is being monopolized. Therefore, I think we ought to be asking the government which has introduced this bill why more has not been done, and why it does not propose that Canada take a giant leap forward in assisting people to go into business and stay in business or to undertake family farming.
We certainly welcome the fact the government proposes that legislation in respect of small businesses loans should be changed so that loans will become available to businesses grossing $1 million a year and loans increased to $50,000. But when we realize that since 1961, when the small business loans system was introduced by the previous Progressive Conservative government, in all that time only $290 million in loans has been provided, the highest record for a year being one in which $30 million was made available to small businessmen, we see how triflingly little this small business loans administration means to the small business people of Canada.
I think it is evident to anyone who looks at the spending record of the government that this is almost nothing at all when compared with what the government puts into LIP, OFY and all the other alphabet soup organizations which have been funded with hundreds of millions of dollars. We then begin to see how this bill is in fact nothing more than economic tokenism and I would hope that the House is generally apprised of the benefits these amendments will provide to small businesses and how little they will actually achieve.
I think more benefit would accrue to small businesses if the government would consider some of the measures which I will now suggest. The first is an increase in information services provided by the government to small businessmen seeking financing of this kind. The fact is that all too few men are aware of what is available and all too few find themselves able to make the most of the opportunity that is provided. What we need is the government financing and undertaking an information and public relations program in order that small businessmen
Loans Acts Amendments
and other people willing to go into business will be aware of the financing available to them. Very frequently they have to come to members of parliament or to other public officers and ask for the basic information which should have been made known to them and which too often is almost hidden from them. So I hope the minister will consider this kind of information program as a basic way of helping the small business community to make the most of the financial opportunity that the act provides.
The second thing for which I would hope is that we might add to the incentive program so that greater assistance might be made available to people wanting to undertake the risks of private enterprise. The kind of incentive that could be made available is analogous to the kind of incentive that has been given to the big corporations, incentive that has been given through the various tax write-offs that are now part of our economy. If these are justified for big corporations, surely something comparable should be available to small businessmen, not necessarily in the manufacturing or the processing industries but those which play a vital part in the economy through the various small service companies they provide. I would hope that much more in the way of tax incentives could be made available to these people.
In my own municipality, the borough of Scarborough, part of metro Toronto, the industrial register indicates somewhat in excess of 1,800 different companies and firms doing business. One is impressed in looking through that register to see that the vast majority of those businesses employ fewer than 25 people. Basically, our municipality is comprised of very small companies and one-man firms. These people are providing the majority of the jobs available in that community but they are having the greatest difficulty staying in business. They need tax incentives, they need financial assistance and all too little of it is being provided by the government under the present legislation.
A third recommendation that I would make to the government is simply to get off the backs of the ordinary small businessmen and give them an opportunity to do their daily work without having to spend so much time working for the government. One of the complaints made most frequently to me by the small businessmen in the community I represent concerns the time they have to devote to answering questionnaires, filling out forms and tabulating statistics, all at no charge to the government but at their own cost. This work often is done by the businessman himself or by his wife at night, on weekends or in the little spare time they have available to provide the government with information which the government may or may not use.

I hope that, not only for economic reasons but much more for social reasons, we in parliament will find the opportunity to take that leap forward.
Important as the small business community is economically, it is of even greater significance socially. speechtext:
that Bill C-19, to amend the Canada Pension Plan, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-19 is the second important bill amending the Canada Pension Plan introduced by the government in the House within a year that is since, in co-operation with the provinces, it undertook a reform of the social security system in Canada. The first bill was passed by Parliament during the last session. Among other things, it provided pension increases from 8 to 20 per cent to some 500,000 contributors to the plan, it guaranteed full rise of present and future allowances on the basis of the future increases in the cost of living and finally it set the ceiling of acceptable earnings under the plan for the years 1974 and 1975.
Provided it meets with the approval of Parliament, the bill in question today would implement the commitments made through the first series of agreements on the Canada Pension Plan reached in Ottawa with the provinces in October 1973. Similarly, this bill would also implement the second series of federal-provincial agreements arrived at two months ago at the Edmonton conference. The main points of the bill to be studied today could be summarized thus:
1.	It would provide for complete equality of status of all contributors and beneficiaries under the Canada Pension Plan, whether male or female;
2.	It would do away with the means test and the criterion according to which the eligibility of a contributor to a pension is determined; this means that persons of 65 and more would be entitled to a retirement pension regardless of what money they might earn at a later date;
3.	It sets out a formula for the calculation of maximum eligible earnings under the plan, that is the year's maximum pensionable earnings, so that levels of benefits and cash receipts may reflect increased salary rates as witnessed in the past decade. Under that formula once an adequate basis for the calculation of levels of benefits and cash receipts is brought up-to-date it will then be possible to align that basis on the average salaries and wages of workers in Canadian industry;
4.	It would amend the present formula used to determine the annual basic exemption under the plan; that formula would have the advantage of giving greater access to Canadians on lower incomes who could then fully participate in the Canada Pension Plan;
5.	It would reintroduce for approval by Parliament the provisions set out in Bill C-190 which would exclude from the plan certain categories of people who would wish not to participate on the grounds of their religious beliefs; the provisions dealing with the reimbursement of legal expenses would be softened, and certain other steps would be taken with respect to the financial administration of the plan and the negotiation of international agreements.

Although they received very favourable support from Parliament those proposals could not be passed before the end of the last session.
6.	Finally, it incorporates many technical amendments to correct a few minor mistakes and certain ambiguities or anomalies which can be found in the present text and which the department responsible for the implementation of the plan noted lately. In principle the technical amendments would not affect most contributors and recipients but it would be a different case altogether for those who are directly concerned, and those corrections would benefit almost all those people.
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will obviously have noted, when I pointed out earlier that the passage of Bill C-19 would respect the commitments made under the first and second series of agreements concluded with the provinces, that I deliberately avoided using the word "final" in speaking of these series of agreements.
In my opinion, the Canada Pension Plan revision is far from being definitely completed. Among the other priorities that we have yet to settle and that we are considering in this regard, and I am thinking among other things about the provisions that have to be brought in to ensure coverage under the plan for housewives, about suggestions advocating preretirement, about the need for having clear-cut levels of disability and survival benefits, and last but non least about this other question being raised concerning invalids, orphans, widows and widowers, that is to what extent would the needs of these persons be best met through social insurance programs, such as the Canada Pension Plan, rather than through income supplement plans?
As to the participation of the homemakers, I had the opportunity of discussing the matter with my provincial counterparts during our last meeting in February, at Edmonton. I should rightfully say that we have all acknowledged the complexity of the problems caused by the various proposals concerning the participation of homemakers. So we thought it would be unwise to try to draw hasty conclusions before being able to carry through the overall examination of every aspect of the problem.
Nevertheless, we agreed upon the advantages of certain alternatives, among which voluntary contributions and pension credit sharing would surely deserve a thorough review in 1974.
We shared the view that it would certainly be desirable that a public debate be held on this matter and all related aspects. Finally, we decided to refer it to the advisory committee on the Canada Pension Plan as well as the advisory committee on the status of women for consideration and additional comments.
I would say in addition that I think it is most important to put this matter before the House and for this purpose, I filed a few days ago before the standing committee on health, welfare and social affairs a document intitled "Housewives and the Canada Pension Plan".
In this regard, I read with the highest interest in last Tuesday's Hansard the debate about the private bill put forward by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) and in particular the suggestion of the hon. members for Waterloo-Cambridge and Vancouver Kings-
April 16, 1974

way (Mrs. Maclnnis) that the old age security plan might well prove to be a more efficient mechanism than the Canada Pension Plan as regards housewive's contribution.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do hope that these measures will be subjected to more discussion, both within and without Parliament, and that these debates will bring about valuable solutions. At the same time, research will continue on the studies I mentioned and I have every reason to believe that they will be successfully completed within the time limits we have set to achieve the review of the social security system in Canada. Though it may be too early to foretell the results of these studies as well as other studies that will be carried out in this area, they might call for the introduction of a third bill that would provide for further amendments to the Canada Pension Plan.
With your leave, Mr. Speaker, I would now deal with the provisions of Bill C-19 that in my opinion are the most important.
The most noteworthy changes proposed by the bill, in terms of principle, are the provisions for the equal treatment of male and female contributors and beneficiaries, and I take particular pleasure in being able to include them in this bill. The equal treatment of Canadian men and women is, of course, a principle to which this government is firmly committed, and is being reflected in further legislation to be considered during the current session of parliament.
The discussion paper I recently tabled in the House Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs states:
This is a time of reappraisal concerning the position of women in society and in the home. Certain traditional assumptions and values are being questioned and changed. This relates both to the increasing participation of women in the economic work force of the nation, and to changing attitudes concerning the position of women within the fundamental unit of Canadian society-the family.
Bill C-19 provides striking and tangible evidence of the rate and degree to which traditional assumptions and attitudes on the role of women in Canadian society have changed. The end of the transitional phase of the Canada Pension Plan still lies about two years off in the future. Yet, before the plan is fully mature, we are already concluding that we should remove the basic distinctions between males and females which were built into the plan with a broad measure of public support only a few short years ago.
What exactly are the distinctions that are to be abolished by Bill C-19? The Canada Pension Plan now provides that upon the death of a male contributor, a surviving widow is automatically eligible for a pension that is equal to 60 per cent of her husband's actual or imputed retirement pension if she is 65 or older. If the surviving widow is between 45 and 65 years of age, or is below the age of 45 and is disabled or has dependent children, she is eligible for a pension that is equal to 37 V4 per cent of her husband's actual or imputed retirement pension plus a flat rate component which now amounts to $33.76 a month. Lesser amounts are paid to widows who are between 35
Canada Pension Plan
and 45 years of age and are not disabled or do not have dependent children.
In addition, when a male contributor dies or becomes disabled, his children automatically become eligible for a benefit that, at present, amounts to $33.76 per month for each child subject to some variation for those in families having more than four children. On the other hand, when a female contributor dies or becomes disabled, her surviving widower is eligible for a widower's pension only if he is disabled and was dependent upon his wife, and the children become eligible for a benefit only if they were "wholly or substantially" maintained by their mother. These differences, it should be noted, have existed notwithstanding the fact that the contribution rate to the plan is the same for male and female contributors.
The bill proposes the complete removal of these distinctions. The effect of this change, if and when enacted, will be that surviving spouses and children of deceased or disabled female contributors will, in future, qualify for the same benefits and under the same conditions as those that now apply in respect of the surviving spouses and children of male contributors. The current provision which limits the payment of one benefit for each child will be maintained and it will be paid upon the death or disability of the first spouse.
I would also like to draw the attention of hon. members to an important clause in the bill that proposes retroactive eligibility, but not retroactive payment, for the surviving spouses and children of female contributors who died or became disabled prior to proclamation of this bill. In other words, the bill proposes that after proclamation, widowers and the children of female contributors who died or became disabled prior to proclamation will from that point in time on become eligible to receive benefits as though the Canada Pension Plan had always accorded equal treatment to male and female contributors and beneficiaries. This particular proposal of the bill will, it is estimated, benefit about 30,000 individuals.
I would like to take this opportunity to remind those who may be affected by this retroactive feature that benefits under the Canada Pension Plan are only payable upon application. I would suggest, therefore, that potential beneficiaries of female contributors "who died or became disabled prior to proclamation of the bill should consult a Canada Pension Plan district office about their eligibility for a benefit as soon after the bill comes into force as possible. I would also propose to draw this to the attention of those who may be affected by this measure by means of inserts in the appropriate federal cheques issued to individuals by the government.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

plish anything. Well, here is our chance. What better week's work than to abolish the Senate between now and six o'clock!

subsubtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 MEASURE TO ABOLISH THE SENATE
speechtext:
As the hon. member on the other side said a moment ago, this is not the first time that I have proposed this measure. Indeed, I have been at it for a good many years. The more I think about it, the more I observe the operations of the other place, the more I consider the meaning of democracy, the more ludicrous I find it that we still have, as part of our law making parliament, a group of 102 men and women who are not elected, who are not responsible to anyone, yet who have the same lawmaking authority that is accorded to those who are elected by the people of Canada.
I can understand that more than 100 years ago, when the constitution of this country was being drawn, it made sense not to trust democracy completely. It made sense, especially with the House of Lords in Britain and such as examples, that there might be a group of detached senior citizens who could take a second look at what the elected people might do. Frankly, sir, I do not think there is a case for that at all any longer. Either we believe in democracy or we do not. Either we believe in the laws of the land being made by persons elected by the people of the country, or we do not, and if we do believe in representative democracy I submit that we should not have, as part of parliament, a non-elected body.
Therefore I propose once again my bill that calls for the abolition of the Senate. Anyone who takes the trouble to look at the bill, which in this session is number C-118, will see that it is a rather lengthy one. That is because the abolition of the Senate calls for a number of consequential changes in the British North America Act. But even after one has studied those consequential changes one will see that all the bill does is to abolish the Senate itself.
Despite what is said about me sometimes in the other place-and the things that are said make interesting reading-I want to say that, in my view, there are some very fine persons in the Senate of Canada. A number of them, in my view, are very conscientious in the work that they endeavour to do.
As one who is around this building a good deal of the time, I can say that there are times, especially over weekends, when conscientious Senators around these halls outnumber members of the House from all parties. But that is not the issue. It does not matter how fine and upstanding the members of the other place might be. It does not matter how much attention they give to the job that is assigned to them. What is wrong in principle is that non-elected persons have the authority of law makers.
I know too that it is sometimes argued that they do great work in committees. In particular it is argued that some of the special committees that are appointed to study problems such as poverty, pensions, land use or matters related to science policy, do good work. That is perfectly true. But it does not justify maintaining 102 individuals on salary, and maintaining an institution at a total cost of something over $7 million a year, so that 15 or 20 of them can do good work on committees. If there are jobs that we want done, jobs of research, jobs of inquiry, it is perfectly
April 16, 1974

possible to set up committees or commissions specifically assigned to do those jobs. I suggest that we can do all of this at much less than the cost of maintaining the Senate.
However, entirely apart from the question of cost, I feel very strongly that any such job that they do does not give Their Honours the right to share equally with us the powers of law making. It is contended sometimes these days-in fact it is contended by some of the more thoughtful members of the other place-that they really do not exercise their veto power; the most they now exercise is a suspensive veto. For example, in the most recent case was the wiretapping legislation.
Senators tried to amend the bill that we had passed in this House, but when in this House we stood our ground, all they did was to have a lengthy debate about it, and in the end they agreed to pass it. I say with respect that I thought that some of them over there stated the case very correctly when they said that they had done their job by entering a suspensive veto, and that it was not their moral right to go all the way and turn down what had been assed in this House. Although I said that with respect, I have to say that it is also an argument against the other place. Why keep an institution that really has no power? It has it constitutionally, but in terms of practice Their Honours have come to realize that they would be unwise to exercise that constitutional power. So in effect, Mr. Speaker, we are maintaining a nullity. I think therefore that we should come up to date and recognize democracy as the basic principle of a parliamentary institution and have in it only persons who are elected by the people of Canada.
Some argue on occasion that the points I have been making call not for the ultimate solution, namely the abolition of the Senate, but rather for reform. Mr. King was a great one for it. The only reform he ever made was to turn a Conservative Senate into a Liberal Senate. Somewhat later Conservative prime ministers tried to reform it the other way, but they did not last long enough.
But to be serious, Mr. Speaker, the most significant reform that some people advocate is to put it on an elective basis. I think we have enough strains and stresses in government in this country already. We have the conflict between the executive and the House of Commons, between government and opposition, and so on. We have the confrontation or the negotiating that has to go on, if you will, between the federal government and the various provincial governments.
I suggest that if we had a second House of this parliament that was elected as we are, and had the same amount of authority as we have, we would slow down the machinery of legislation and the machinery of government to a disturbing extent.
Without taking the time to go into it, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I have thought about the various reforms that might be made, but to me they do not make sense. The argument that the Senate is needed to protect minorities does not grab me. I do not know how we in Manitoba, as a small province, find our minority position protected by the fact that we have six members in the other House. I suggest the place where minorities are best protected is here in this House of Commons where we are responsible
Abolition of the Senate
to the people who elected us, and finally in the courts. All told, I can see no place for the Senate.
I now come back to my earlier remarks and I plead very strongly that what I am saying is not personal with regard to those who are in the other place at the present time. If I said that my observation of their performance leads me to believe it should be abolished, that is because I sense the futility of what they are doing. Over there they sometimes think I am hard on them. They have my sympathy. Their job is so useless. As I say, that does not take away from the sterling qualities of many who are over there. But when it is all added up, I feel there is no real place for the Senate in our parliamentary setup.
A former colleague in my party, and one who was a colleague when we were both engaged in the work of the Canadian Labour Congress, is now over there. I like to read to him or in his presence a memorandum that he wrote some time ago on the Senate. In it he said very clearly that the Senate is the most undemocratic institution in the world. He said it could go on a thousand times vetoing what has been done in the House of Commons, and he clearly took a stand for its abolition. That, of course, was before he became a member of the other place.
I still agree with him, even if he does not!
I thought I had read everything that has been written on the Senate but I learned this afternoon that the Minister of Finance once wrote a thesis on the abolition of the Senate. I asked him to send me a copy of it so that I could include his gems of wisdom the next time I spoke on this issue. I would say that those who speak of this subject approach it not with any feelings against those who are there but on the principle that parliament ought to be a democratic institution, and there ought not to be in it a place where members are responsible to no one. I emphasize that, Mr. Speaker. They are appointed, of course, by the Governor General, but it is really by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who names them. Once a member is appointed he is not even responsible to the Prime Minister and is certainly not responsible to the people of Canada. This does not make sense at all, and that is why I say, Mr. Speaker, that the only sensible thing to do with the Senate is to abolish it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I trust the discrepancy will be rectified in a very short time in order to make the good life more pleasant in these holy surroundings.
I hasten at the outset to express to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) my deepest respect and appreciation for his persistence in this particular matter. I feel that most of the arguments he advances are reasoned and have withstood the test of time. As far as his logic is concerned I would hope that perhaps some of the suggestions he makes would be accepted.
However, last year when I spoke on this topic I indicated to you, Mr. Speaker, that I hoped it was not the beginning of a long tradition, as long as that of the hon.

April 16, 1974
Abolition of the Senate
member for Winnipeg North Centre who had been speaking on this matter for a number of years. I promised that that would be the only time I would speak on the subject, but I find myself again speaking on it and perhaps establishing such a tradition. I might indicate, if this is the way fate should direct, that I will endeavour to reply to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre any time he presents this particular bill.
I would also agree with the hon. member when he states that members of the Senate are intelligent gentlemen and gentlewomen-all of them are-and that he finds in that particular chamber a number of very competent individuals. I am sure that those individuals will not regard his attempts to abolish that honourable House as an indication of his disrespect toward them. However, I take it they would strenuously disagree with the main argument reiterated by the hon. member, that the existence of the Senate as a non-elective body is repugnant to our democratic system.
I might point out to the hon. member that the Queen is part of our government, the Governor General is part of our government-not the government, but the whole parliamentary and constitutional system of Canada. Surely no one can argue that the Governor General, or indeed the Lieutenant Governor of each province is an elected individual, chosen by the people of Canada. They are all appointed.
I might also point out to the hon. gentleman that this institution, a most venerable one which has withstood 600 or 700 years of time, has been established through long tradition and evolution, and indeed is based upon the British parliamentary system. Within that particular system there is a recognition of the work of the House of Lords, which House is very similar to ours, ours having been framed upon the tenets of that House and the traditions established by it.
I had occasion recently to be in England, Mr. Speaker, and spoke to the Lord Chancellor who is the president of that particular upper House. I also had occasion to speak to some of the members of the House of Lords in England, and I suggest to the hon. member that, quite contrary to beliefs that might be held in Canada relating to that House, it is indeed a vital place. It is a place of considerable activity notwithstanding the fact that its powers are limited to a suspensive veto, the same as tradition is establishing that the Senate of Canada be limited to in its powers.
I suggest, further, that the House of Lords considers the Senate of Canada as a model with respect to some of the practices we follow. For example, only life peers are appointed to the House of Lords now. The number of hereditary peers is shrinking. We do the same in our Senate. Senators are appointed until they reach 75. I might suggest that the obligatory retirement age be reduced. Once a Senator reaches the age of 70 perhaps he should be forced to retire from the other place.
As I said in my speech last year, I think the other place was established in Canada to protect the interests of the regions. It provides for regional representation. At present the Senate is not as active as it has been; on the other

hand, it is not as active as it will be. Within a short period it may be necessary for us to have an upper house which is more representative than at present. We are, as you know, dealing with the question of redistribution. The effect of the commissioner's report has been suspended. We are studying, in the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, various methods by which we can secure adequate representation for the various areas of Canada. I suggest that a considerable problem faces Canada in this regard at this time.

If we want adequate representation from sea to sea, it must be able to offer protection and justice to all areas of Canada. Mr. Speaker, the small regions of the country, such as Prince Edward Island, must always be represented in the Senate.
I also believe that some amendments must be introduced. As I said last year, the condition that a citizen must have $4,000 to be appointed to the Senate is, in my opinion, absolutely outmoded. Nothing justifies the fact that someone should be deprived of the honour of sitting in the Senate because he does not have $4,000 in his bank account or any other assets of $4,000. This brings me to the second point. I believe that there are too many senior citizens in the other place.

I suggest that some of the most effective members of this House are senior citizens. Indeed, the member sponsoring this bill has been proud to say he is a senior citizen. Age has nothing to do with one's effectiveness in the legislative process. Speaking as an idealist I hope that younger people will be appointed to the Senate in future. Let those who are between 20 and 40 years old, the age group of the majority of the population, inspire the other place with their contribution.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre well knows, there is a great proportion of younger members serving in this House. I am sure he would not say that the contribution of younger members-perhaps with the exception of yours truly who wants to see this bill defeated-is not substantial and has not brought profit for this House. The same could be said for the other place. We could follow tradition, but appoint younger members.
I suggest that the Upper House, composed of a greater number of younger members, might be empowered only to suspend consideration of certain bills or to request the House of Commons to reconsider certain measures. I do not think it is true to say that the House of sober second thought was meant to be occupied only by older people. I am sure, and I think the House will agree, that younger people can reflect on certain issues and give guidance and direction.
I disagree with the hon. member's contention that minorities are not receiving protection. I am not speaking of regional minorities so much as of ethnic minorities. On the other hand, as I said in my speech last year, there are minorities in Canada which are not sufficiently concentrated in any given area and which do not sufficiently influence our legislative input. They give no input with regard to the legislative process. I suggest that the Senate is one place in which such minorities can be provided with
April 16, 1974

opportunities for input. It is desirable to see the various segments of society represented in Parliament.
Before we reach the stage which is evident in England, where the Trade Union Congress is effectively running the Labour government, where the organized labour movement is standing on the step of power, we should provide for members of organized labour to sit in the Canadian Senate. Let them have some say in the legislative process so that we may defuse any potentially dangerous situation which might develop in future. Also, I see nothing wrong with naming some civil servants to the Senate. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, you will probably have noted that a number of public servants have considerable powers or have had important responsibilities since the beginning of their career as public servants. I do not see why we could not appoint to the Senate certain public servants who would contribute to the Parliament.

I attended a seminar at which an interesting lecture was given by Dame Evelyn Sharp, Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Local Government, in the U.K. She has been contributing actively to the House of Lords, and politicians in that place say that her contribution has been most helpful.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre may not have been helped by a member of the other place, as few supporters of his party have been appointed to the other place. I, on the other hand, have been helped considerably by members of the Senate in matters affecting my responsibilities in this House. Those particular individuals had at one time participated in the deliberations of this House, and they offered valuable guidance to a new member. It is no secret that Liberal members of the Senate participate in our caucus deliberations. We find their contribution most helpful-

I am not blaming them. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) suggests that perhaps I was trying to blame them for something. I was not. I could name people who have been most helpful to me, to other members of the House and, indeed, to the government. As the Leader of the Opposition knows, there is a dearth of elected members on this side representing a certain province in this country. But some Senators are most cognizant of the social and economic conditions in that particular province. I have no hesitation in approaching them when I want information that is not otherwise readily available. A whole range of services is rendered by members of that House. I am not going to hide the fact we have benefited from members of that House who have been active in that House and active in political organizations. I do not hide that fact. If anyone finds objection with that he would find objection with the whole political process. Indeed, we need to have elections and we need to have political organization.
Surely if one can acquit himself of those responsibilities and also acquit himself of legislative responsibilities
Abolition of the Senate
imposed by a House of parliament, I can see no conflict there, or anything with which one can take issue. Perhaps I am a bit conservative with regard to that particular issue.

I feel there are numerous amendments that should be presented. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that we have been mouthing the question of the necessity of amending the Senate for years. I suggest, however, that we can change our practices now without the necessity of substantial amendments.
As I pointed out to the hon. member last year, we still need to get this particular bill through the Senate. I also pointed out that the suicidal instincts in that particular place are not common. I am sure they are not rampant. They would not attempt to do away with themselves with one fell swoop of the pen.
In view of that particular reality I suggest we should be putting pressure on the government, whether this or some future one, to change its attitude with regard to staffing the other place. We ought not to waste our time, and I say this most respectfully, in the tilting of windmills. We should be using those methods available to us in order to effect those changes that are essential and that ought to bt effected.
I do not want to use all my arguments. I will have to use other arguments next year. I attempted today to complement the arguments I made last year. In case the hon. member has forgotten, last year I stressed the question of ethnic representation to a considerable extent. This year I could stress the fact that we need more young people in the Senate. I am not trying to find myself a spot. I have no interest in sitting in the Senate. In any event I do not think I am eligible at this stage.

speechtext:
That sounds very reasonable, if one follows the hon. member's argument to the fullest extent. I suggest to the hon. member that the Senate does not exercise the power which this House exercises. I agree that constitutionally, save and except for money bills, it has equal or parallel power. However, and I am sure the hon. member will agree with this as well, in practice the other place does not exercise that power. As a matter of fact, the power Senators exercised with regard to the wiretap bill was indeed an aberration from their past practice. There is no doubt in the mind of anyone in this House, except perhaps that of the hon. member, that in the future the Senate will not employ those powers that are afforded to it under the constitution.
In my view there is no difficulty in the fact there may be some Senators from the province of Alberta who sit in the Liberal caucus and are perhaps able to indicate, in the absence of other members, what feelings might be in that province. They may be able to render service in that manner. That does not mean there is any member in this House from Alberta who sits in this particular party. Nor do they have a legislative influence in this particular House.
If I call a Senator's constituent in the province of Alberta in order to seek advice relating to a particular matter which is before this House-and I understand we are going to be studying a bill affecting oil and the administration of an oil policy-I cannot see how that could be detrimental to my particular function. Whether that person is in Alberta or sitting in the Senate, I fail to see the difference.
