Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the last exchange it went through my mind that one of the glories of the other place is that there is no time limit on speeches.
I indicated to the venerable and honourable member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) two years ago that I might support him in 23 years time. Now, at the age of 54, I think I will need to have another 21 years before I jump to the support of such a suggestion.

subsubtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 MEASURE TO ABOLISH THE SENATE
speechtext: Sober second thought.

subsubtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 MEASURE TO ABOLISH THE SENATE
speechtext:
Yes. After two years of thinking it over, I am still reluctant to agree with him. The hon. member and I agree on many important things, but I think our disagreement today indicates the basic difference between a doctrinaire and a pragmatic reformer. A doctrinaire looks at an institution in society. If he does not find it working perfectly or extremely well, he says scrap it. The pragmatic reformer, the base and core of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, looks at an institution in society, either political or economic, and says the criterion is performance; therefore we come forward with suggestions to improve it.
It strikes me as an exercise in fatalism to say there is not sufficient ingenuity in the Canadian political province to develop in the Senate a place that is workable, valuable, and contributes importantly to our political process.
As the hon. member mentioned, this whole question of bicameralism is an old story. Most political organizations have decided on bicameral legislatures. There have been a

variety of suggestions for change. Down through history some have become unicameral and have gone back to bicameralism.
I think the hon. member mentioned some of the functions which have been performed by another type of element in our political structure. The primacy, of course goes to the elected one accepting representative responsibility. That is fundamental. However, there are many parts of the governmental structure, and these were alluded to by the hon. member who preceded me, which are not of that kind. In the whole process the Senate fits in as something between that at the apex and that which is at the foundation, that is the ground and the elected House.
I believe that instead of tossing out the Senate we should ask for some good will and some wisdom in the appointment of the members thereof, and put that illustrious body to more work. I have often thought there are far too many legislative schemes launched in this House. Much could be done over there. When you are faced with a bill of 117 pages, and an agenda such as is usually before us in this portion of the parliamentary year, the situation surely calls for more spadework to be done over there.
I, too, join the hon. member in praising some of the excellent work which has been done by the Senate committees. I believe the Senate foreign affairs study on the Caribbean Commonwealth is one of the finest examinations ever conducted in an important area of Canadian foreign policy. I go back to the old question which Sir George Foster raised long before I was born, before even the hon. member was born-God help us, it is a long time ago. But he said: "End it or mend it." I am not so bereft of hope as to believe there is no possibility of mending it. I am not suggesting it is only a matter of a few judicious and thoughtful appointments from this place to the other place, although the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) is here. But, of course, it is a matter of personnel.
One amusing remark was made by the speaker who moved this motion, though he did not look upon the subject as being a humorous one. He said he felt sympathy for Senators. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have looked at those Senators all my life and I have never felt they were objects of sympathy. Envy, perhaps, but not sympathy. At the tender age of 54 I would not go along with the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) in suggesting that there be some changes in the age limits, both upward and downward. A man of 30 is not really an oldtimer, and you can get in there when you are 30. As to the $4,000, naturally, as an impecunious professor I am not in favour of scrapping that. But, on a more serious note, the need is to look more realistically and more carefully at the structure and basis of representation.
More consideration ought to be given to the provinces as units, and a structural limitation might be placed upon the untrammelled choice open to Prime Ministers, far too many of whom have looked upon it as an exercise in the most sophisticated patronage. It is not the institution, it is the way in which the institution has been caused to function. Because I wish to hear from some of my hon. friends I shall say only, by way of conclusion that I believe the hon. member is a little too reckless, a little too
April 16, 1974

lacking in faith when he decides no one has sufficient ingenuity to make that part of parliament work. Even if his party is bereft of hope, the rest of us surely believe we could do a good job if given a chance.
It could be made a fine and noble second chamber, perhaps not equal to the Senate of Rome or to the Senate of the United States, but it could still be an effective institution and a functional adornment of our structure.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened to debates on this subject for many years before I sat in this chamber. I did so from the gallery to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pointed just a few minutes ago. It is interesting that I should be here now to take part in such a debate myself, because having heard the hon. member express his views on other occasions, and since I am honoured by having him as a neighbour, an occasional chauffeur and an occasional adviser, and I dare say, as a friend in the parliamentary sense-

subsubtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 MEASURE TO ABOLISH THE SENATE
speechtext: Don't forget the snow shoveling you do for me!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT, 1867 MEASURE TO ABOLISH THE SENATE
speechtext:
Yes. Believe it or not we even have a half interest in the same snowblower.
Anyway I did not think I would be discussing this particular topic with my hon. friend and speaking against the principle which the bill before us seeks to advance. I am concerned because what we are witnessing today is the spectacle of one institution of parliament, namely the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, attempting to destroy another institution of parliament, and I do not think this is a very healthy situation.
If we are disposed to talk about the legislative process it should not be to tear down an institution but to enrich its processes. The hon. member himself indicated that the Senate has performed a number of very useful functions.
I find myself agreeing with most of what the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) said. To that extent I find myself in strange company, but I suppose one does find oneself in strange company from time to time. When we deal with parliamentary institutions we ought to look to the improvement and enrichment of those institutions. We must seek to bring to bear upon the legislative process an expression of the interests which go to make up this country.
One of the things that moved the Fathers of Confederation to agree upon the establishment of a Senate was that
Abolition of the Senate
provision in some way for representation on a regional basis was probably a prerequisite to confederation in 1867. I think they were wise in reaching that decision; they were wise to recognize that the particular constitutional make up which was required would not be secure if members of both bodies were elected. So they determined that the various regions of that day would be represented by an appointed house.
As the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) has said, if the public mind has altered with respect to the Senate it is not because of the institution itself but possibly because of the way in which its members have been appointed, that is to say, places in the Senate have been regarded as a reward in many cases for qualities other than excellence in fields which are important to our country.
I think prime ministers should remember that it is not only publishers of newspapers, not only lawyers, not only industrialists, not only loyal party workers who have made this country great. There are a lot of unsung heroes in the cultural endeavours of our people, in science, and in the professions. And perhaps those who have contributed in an occupational or professional sense to the development of Canada have not been rewarded; instead, rewards have gone to others who, in the eyes of many people, seem less deserving. It is as a result of this that the institution has perhaps fallen in the esteem of the public, prompting the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to move that the institution be abolished.
I think the hon. member for Hillsborough has made a very good point. He followed along the argument made by the hon. member for Nipissing that we ought not to tear down or destroy an institution that is a place of very sober second thought on how we improve our legislative process. It is still a very real thing in Canada to protect, in terms of representation and as an expression in the legislative sense of varying viewpoints, particularly the minorities in this country. Indeed, we live in a democracy, but sometimes the democratic process does not work to protect minorities. This is one way in which this institution, responsibly used in regard to the appointments made to it, can protect minority interests.
I am certain that the most important reason that has been advanced during this debate for the maintenance of the Senate, and certainly for its enhancement, is the matter raised by the hon. member for Nipissing, namely, the very troubling and vexing problem of redistribution, and the fact that in our time there are diminishing populations in certain areas and growing populations in others. Through the Senate an attempt can be made to maintain some sort of balance. So, under those circumstances I do not think that we ought to tamper with something as traditional to our constitution and to our country as the Queen, and as the office of the Governor General. In fact such attempts should be withstood and avoided.
Perhaps we should look at the other side of the coin and see how we can enrich an office mentioned by the hon. member for Nipissing, the office of the Governor General. I suppose in modern political parlance, in the practical sense the Governor General of this country has no real

April 16, 1974
Abolition of the Senate
power. As a result of what I might call-this is not an apt description-very impressive and responsible appointments made to that office by the Queen, upon the recommendation of her Privy Councillors in Canada, all the incumbents of that office have grown in affection and regard in the minds of the public of Canada. I do not think there is anyone in this chamber who would say that merely because that office is an appointed office it has become useless, and that nothing is served by it.
I look upon the Senate not as a resting place for retired politicians but as a proper reward, and necessarily so, for real service to one's country. It is a place where the unsung heroes of Canada- the scientist who has made a contribution, the parliamentarian who has made a contribution, members of the agricultural community and others, and indeed members in legislative fields other than the federal field-can find an opportunity to continue their service, and in an area where, perhaps because of the nature of the political process, they could not venture to perform this kind of service.
But for the service of many Senators, both before and during their appointments, our country would not be as rich and as full in terms of the quality of its legislative assemblies as it is today. I do not believe that that opportunity has passed us by. I do not believe that the time has come when we ought to say that it is not possible for us to enrich the body politic by the proper use of a chamber of sober second thought, indeed perhaps by a new kind of approach to the legislative process that really has not been tried.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said something to the effect that if we believe in democracy then we ought not to support a body that, by its nature, is appointed. If we speak in those terms we must relate them to the Canadian situation. There was a great lesson to be learned from the work of the Fathers of Confederation. We must not forget that there are perhaps people and areas in this country that would not be represented but for the existence of the Senate.
I hope that in considering this bill the House will move to enrich the nation and this institution of parliament. I urge upon those who, from time to time have authority to make Senate appointments, to make those appointments carefully so that they are representative of all the major groups in the country, of all the political affiliations in this country, and thus uphold democratic principles. I hope that out of this process will arise a vital, strong second chamber that will take a new place in our Canadian democracy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was interrupted at five o'clock I had given some information concerning one of the major clauses of this particular bill, that is the clause which eliminates discrimination on the basis of sex under the Canada Pension Plan as it stands at the present time.
Before moving to another major area of the bill I should like to elaborate briefly on the statement I made at the beginning of my remarks this afternoon in respect of survivors' benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. We are at the moment reviewing the structure and level of these benefits and as I agreed with my provincial colleagues in Edmonton, "it is necessary to examine the most appropriate approach to the provision of survivor benefits, whether under the two pension plans, or under a new and general economic support program," the two pension plans being the Quebec Pension Plan and the Canada Pension Plan.
We are, for example, asking ourselves about the role that a flat rate component should play in Canada Pension Plan survivor benefits in the future, and whether there is any merit in considering its transfer from the Canada Pension Plan to a new and general economic support program. These studies have not been completed, and so the government's position on these questions has not yet been formed. I should like to assure the House that when the eventual position of the government is formed, and if it requires legislative action by the House, it will be advanced in terms that preserve the principle of equality now being built into the plan, that is equality between the two sexes.

Another major series of amendments incorporated in Bill C-19 seek to eliminate the provisions dealing with the employment test and the retirement criteria under which eligibility is determined.
Indeed, under the present provisions of the act only those contributors between the ages of 65 and 70 who have retired from their regular employment may claim full value of pension under the Canada Pension Plan. In other words, the pensioner under 70 who, although retired from his regular employment continues to receive earnings exceeding $95 a month automatically gets a reduced pension by 50 per cent of his employment income falling between $95 and $155 and by the full amount of earnings exceeding $155. Those limitations would be repealed under the bill now before us so that if it is passed by this House any contributor 65 or over would be sure to get the full
April 16, 1974

value of his pension, regardless of the employment income he could otherwise receive.
According to my estimates those amendments would immediately result in increased pension levels for about 5,000 recipients now retired and add to the anticipated number of recipients under the Canada Pension Plan for 1975 roughly 30,000 contributors who would then be entitled to the retirement pension. Of course, those between the ages of 65 and 70 would still be free not to claim their retirement pension and continue to pay contributions into the fund and so accumulate further pension credits. A number of contributors will certainly find that option more advantageous.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with the provision governing maximum pensionable earnings, that is; the ceiling as to pensionable earnings under this plan.
My colleagues in the House are certainly aware that maximum pensionable earnings considerably affect the very structure of benefit levels as well as the inflow of money into the Canada Pension Plan fund.
At the federal-provincial conference which was held last October, it was agreed by all welfare ministers that the ceiling as to earnings under the Canada Pension Plan should be in line with the present ceiling under the Quebec Pension Plan, and then increased by 12 Vi per cent annually, until it reached the average earning level for the Canadian worker in the industrial sector.
The first stage was reached when, during last session, Parliament passed a bill which provided for maximum pensionable earnings of $6,600 and $7,400 for 1974 and 1975 respectively. Some provisions of Bill C-19 aim at confirming other clauses of the agreement with projections on the future.
I think it is fair to say that Bill C-19, together with the bill passed in the last session, go a long way toward establishing fair and equitable treatment for the nation's retired, disabled, widows, widowers and orphans. Maximum initial retirement pensions under the plan now stand at $101.41 a month. If the bill is passed, initial maximum CPP retirement pensions should reach a level of about $250 a month by 1980, and $350 by 1985. This represents an increase of close to 250 per cent in about ten years' time.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
May I say to the hon. member who just spoke that this has nothing to do with inflation. Whatever inflation will take place it will be over and above the amounts mentioned here. The amounts I am going to mention strictly apply to the increase in the yearly maximum pensionable earnings, and also the increase that is likely to take place in the average industrial composite in this country coming from Statistics Canada. Those figures have nothing to do with inflation. Whatever rate of inflation may take place over the next ten years, the plan has been indexed last year by an amendment passed in the House which includes automatic indexing to take into account cost of living increases.
Canada Pension Plan
Maximum CPP disability pensions now stand at $125.95 a month. Passage of the bill should raise these pensions to about $225 a month by 1980, and $315 a month by 1985. This represents an increase of close to 170 per cent in 10 years' time.
Maximum CPP widow and widower pensions for beneficiaries under the age of 65 now stand at $79.86 a month. Passage of the bill should raise these pensions to about $135 a month by 1980, and $185 a month by 1985. This represents an increase of over 130 per cent in ten years' time.
Maximum CPP widow and widower pensions for beneficiaries at 65 years of age and over now stand at $73.75 a month. Passage of this bill should raise these pensions to about $145 a month by 1980 and $210 a month by 1985. This represents an increase of over 180 per cent in 10 years time.
As to basic orphan and disabled contributor child benefits, this bill proposes that in the future they should also be paid in respect of the children of female contributors who have died or have become disabled.
I should mention again that all of these increased benefit rates, once they go into pay, would of course be fully escalated thereafter according to increases in the cost of living. It should also be noted that in 1985 we are likely to have three times the 500,000 CPP beneficiaries that we now have.
Before anyone jumps to the conclusion that benefit increases will only apply to those who have earnings at or near the proposed earning ceilings, I would like to state that this will not be the case. In addition, I would like to demonstrate how the updating of the earnings formula that is now in the plan will operate to pass on improvements proposed in Bill C-19 to contributors at lower income levels. The updating formula very simply provides that all contributor earnings are updated according to movements in the yearly maximum pensionable earnings, and so sharp increases in the YMPE produce a sharp updating of past earnings at all levels.
Perhaps I could illustrate this feature by tracing the effect of the bill on a contributor whose earnings never reach the ceilings that would have prevailed had the original CPP legislation not been changed. For this purpose I will relate the bill to a contributor who had earnings of $4,000 in 1966, experiences a steady increase in his earnings to $5,000 a year by 1974, and to $7,000 in 1985 when he retires at the age of 65.
Had the initial plan not been changed this contributor would have received a retirement pension of $162 a month. If the bill is passed this contributor will receive a retirement pension of $223 a month, which is equal to about 40 per cent of his final year's earnings. If an OAS pension for the contributor and his spouse is added to this amount, total CPP/OAS payments for this family will be just about equal to the final year's earnings of the contributor. I might add that the bill also has the effect of slightly reducing the contributions that this contributor will have to make to receive his increased CPP retirement pension. Similar examples can be developed for the effect of the bill on other CPP benefits for lower income contributors.

April 16, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
I take this opportunity to draw the attention of the House also to the fact that the figures I mentioned before are completely independent of whatever payments our retired people are going to receive over the next ten years in terms of old age security payments, so that whatever happens with the OAS it is going to be over and above the various figures I have mentioned here.
These increases, with CPP benefits that I have just cited, in my view are quite substantial but still they do not tell the full story of the achievement that has been realized in our social security reforms.
During the last year other parts of our social security system have been modernized, and when these improvements are combined with Bill C-19 they produce results of almost dramatic proportions.
Consider, for example, the income situation of a couple at retirement in a single wage earner family. A little over a year ago the maximum CPP/OAS income of this couple was about $245 a month; today it is $320 a month. In 1980 it may be in excess of $525 per month, and in 1985 it should be in the order of $700 a month. I might remind hon. members that $700 a month is reasonably close to the average wage of today's industrial worker.
I invite hon. members also to reflect upon the situation of the widow under 65 years of age with four children under the age of 18. A little over a year ago her CPP survivor benefit and family allowance payments would have amounted to about $200 a month; today they are about $295 a month; in 1980, they should be over $400 a month; and in 1985, they could be in the order of $550 a month. This government, I believe, is justified in taking pride in this record of achievement.

A moment ago, I was illustrating the advantages offered by this bill, which could be turned into account by contributors in lower income brackets, but there is more. Other particular provisions will enable people who have a very low income to benefit as well from these advantages.
As my distinguished colleagues in this House certainly know, the Canada Pension Plan provides an exemption on contributory earnings, the year's basic exemption whose level determines the level of earnings a person must be able to prove to be eligible to the Canada Pension Plan. This exemption now amounts to 12 per cent of the ceiling of eligible earnings. According to this formula, in the event of a sudden increase in the ceiling of earnings, a good many contributors in lower income brackets would temporarily be left aside and, consequently, they could not benefit from some advantages offered in this bill.
Thus, in order to prevent such a possibility, we propose to amend the rate on which the year's basic exemption is now calculated by dropping this rate to 10 per cent of maximum eligible earnings. This measure would provide a better opportunity for persons with a low income to take full part in the Canada Pension Plan.
Moreover the bill proposes the repeal of a particular provision which now applies to the self-employed. According to this provision, this person must be able to prove earnings exceeding by one and one third the year's basic
[Mr. Lalonde.j
exemption specified for other contributors. It is thus proposed to cancel this requirement so that employees and self-employed can be dealt with on an equal footing as far as the basic annual exemption is concerned. This measure, Mr. Speaker, would certainly be welcomed by a certain group of self-employed whose seasonal work sometimes depends on fluctuations in earnings which can reduce their income to a marginal level.
In particular, we are thinking of the farmers and fishermen who would like, even in adverse circumstances, not to stop their contributions to the Canada Pension Plan. [English]
The next group of proposals I would like to discuss are those which parliament considered in its debate on Bill C-190 last session, and which are all included in Bill C-19. The most noteworthy of these is the proposal to allow individual members of religious groups to exempt themselves from the operation of the Canada Pension Plan in the case of religious organizations which existed before 1966, which have established tenets opposing the acceptance of benefits from any private or public insurance, and which have the established practice of providing for the support of their dependent members.
As I recall, Mr. Speaker, some hon. members had reservations about this proposal, but it is also my impression that the basic principle behind it engaged the sympathy of the large majority of members of the House. I might say that the government still firmly believes in the universal application of programs such as the Canada Pension Plan but, on balance, considers that the exemption should be made because it is in keeping with the strong traditions of freedom and tolerance that exist in this country.
Another significant clause that is included in this package is a proposal to allow the retroactive application of international agreements concluded by Canada with respect to the Canada Pension Plan. The immediate objective of this change is to enable those Canadians who were employed by the United States at Goose Bay to participate in the plan with effect from July 1, 1972, in accordance with the Canada/United States agreement respecting the transfer of the Goose Bay base to Canadian jurisdiction.
Other significant clauses in this category of proposals include provisions to liberalize features dealing with the payment of legal expenses in appeal proceedings, and to give the Auditor General explicit authority to conduct an annual audit of the Canada Pension Plan account and investment fund.
The remaining proposals in the bill, which are quite numerous, can be labelled as miscellaneous, technical and administrative amendments. I thought I would take the opportunity presented by this bill to carry out some housecleaning in what is a very complex act. Hon. members will find that these proposals, for the most part, rectify inequities, anomalies, errors and ambiguities that have been uncovered over a period of time.
In recent months a number of newspaper articles have appeared drawing attention to the difficulties and situations sometimes created when the department adjusts interim CPP benefit payments. As most hon. members are aware, the law requires us to begin paying CPP benefits when eligibility for them is established, even though the
April 16, 1974

final determination of earnings may not have been settled. I do not think that anyone would suggest that we should do otherwise.
It can take around two years to make a final determination of official earnings, since this involves the filing and processing of income tax returns. Clearly it would be ridiculous to expect a person to wait that long before receiving his regular benefit cheques. Nevertheless, this does mean that benefits often have to be adjusted when final earnings figures become available.
In many instances we find that we have underpaid an individual, but this is no problem because the individual concerned will receive a pleasant surprise when the extra payment arrives in the mail.
As might be expected, we find that in some instances overpayments have occurred and the law requires us to recover them. To provide some relief in such situations, the bill contains a provision that would enable the minister to write off such debts in cases where the debt is uncollectable, where the cost of collection would be in excess of the amount to be recovered, or where the minister is satisfied that recovery action would create undue hardship for the individual. This amendment is proposed to enable us to be as fair and humane in the administration of the plan as we can possibly be.
We also find that in some instances the overpayments are more apparent than real, because the department's record of the contributor's earnings is in error. At the present time, employee corrections in records of earnings must be made within a four-year period. The bill proposes relaxation of this time limit, and in this way it will provide further assurance for contributors and their dependents that they will receive all of the CPP benefits that have been earned. The bill also proposes repeal of the current prohibition that prevents persons who do not have their social insurance number from receiving Canada Pension Plan benefits.
I wish to mention other important technical and administrative proposals contained in the bill. They include:
1.	A series of proposals to improve the plan's appeal system. These include an extension of appeal rights to representatives of contributors and beneficiaries; more generous provision for the payment of legal expenses; and provision for the appointment of a vice-chairman of the Pension Appeals Board.
2.	A proposal to allow the payment of disabled contributor child benefits for natural and legally adopted children acquired by pensioners after the onset of disability.
3.	A proposal to permit payment of Canada Pension Plan benefits to common-law spouses on a more realistic basis.
4.	A proposal to relieve self-employed persons from remitting Canada Pension Plan contributions on an instalment basis if they are not required to remit income tax payments on that basis. This list does not exhaust all of the technical and good housekeeping proposals that are in the bill, but it covers the more significant ones. I think it would be preferable if the remaining ones were discussed during the detailed consideration of the bill in the stand-
Canada Pension Plan
ing committee to which the bill will be referred. As a matter of fact I may have a few additional technical amendments to introduce at that stage as a result of representations received from the provinces after they have had an opportunity to review the bill in detail.
I would like to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that I consider that Bill C-19 is an imaginative and responsible approach to bringing the Canada Pension Plan into harmony with contemporary values and attitudes in Canadian society. I consider that the bill will bring the plan into line with the economic facts of Canadian life now, and in the future. Furthermore, if the bill is passed into law, it will allow the Canada Pension Plan to play a vital role in the new charter the government is writing for this country's aged, disabled, widows, widowers, orphans, and those in need. I hope that the bill will attract the overwhelming support of Canadians inside and outside of Parliament.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I begin by giving the minister a hint that this measure will pass. It is in no danger of being rejected. It is safer by far than a budget, infinitely safer than an opposition day, and perhaps a little safer than the football bill.
The minister closed his speech with what I thought was a flight of imagination when he described the bill as imaginative and responsible. I do not find much in it that is imaginative. Actually, there is little in this amendment or this massive statute that is highly imaginative. This is one of the most difficult and complicated piece of legislation to which my attention has ever been drawn. That does not surprise me, as I was here when this statute and its predecessors went in and out of drydock, so to speak, two or three times before being accepted.
The statute still needs a good deal of refining; it is still a very awkward piece of legislation. It is difficult for laymen who try to understand its provisions to understand where they fit in under the statute. The minister has done well and wisely in seizing this opportunity to make such corrections and ameliorations of anomalies as he has done. There is still much preening and pruning ahead, and it is important that this be done with this massive, comprehensive piece of legislation.
The minister began where we should all begin. He referred to the full equality of treatment for male and female beneficiaries. Although he pointed out how quickly the discrimination was removed, we should all admit and confess that a charge could be levied against us because the discrimination was there in the first place. I agree with what I took to be the minister's appraisal of our social development in this country. I agree that, in recent years, we have been more aware of the nonsense which society has asked us to condone for far too long. I believe that those in our society who have given leadership in this particular field are to be commended. I am certain that this is just one of many pieces of legislation in which we will find a delayed recognition of the equality of the sexes.
Before I sit down, and I will not make a long speech despite the excitement about the Senate this afternoon, I will point out as best I may to the minister that this measure still has a long way to go before it gives both sexes full equality. Of course, in the technical sense, what is said is correct.

April 16, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
The second point I bring up is the situation facing that group between 65 and 70 years of age with regard to the long standing, demeaning means test. I referred to this subject more than once in the last session. I have asked, previously, why in the world should the old chap over 90 work as much as he likes and not have his means diminished, whereas the younger man who happens to be 69 and works suffers because he earns money. This is intolerable in a contributory pension system and is a terrible disincentive to productivity, activity and employment. So, we certainly salute that which we called for one year ago and are delighted to see the provision included in the bill.
I welcome too, as I think any sensible Canadian would, the improved formula for allowing those Canadians at the lower income level to draw benefits from this important piece of legislation. There is a large group which wanted to be involved in the plan, but for which involvement was prohibited because of the levels of income provided for in the statute.
The minister spoke this evening about that portion of last session's Bill C-190 which has to do with an exemption for certain religious groups. Last year, speaking for our party, I expressed the view that this was a right, just, proper, and fitting attitude to take.
At that time I referred to some of the groups mentioned. I expressed respect, and indeed envy at the way in which the groups to which reference was made in the legislation were able in our contemporary society to carry on the old way, with the cherished traditions of our general society a few generations ago. They care for their own aged and their own infirm. They have the ability to look after their own loved ones without turning to the cold, institutionalized care for the aged and senior citizens. People who are able to do this stand tall in society. They are able to put into practical and tangible terms the familial ties of affection and love. That is to be commended.
Another thing I mentioned was with particular reference to the Mennonite community. I said I knew of no group which showed greater charity, concern and interest for the problems of other people all across the world.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Where there is drought, famine and what have you, there is a representative of the Mennonite community there. Since I spoke last year I happened to have been in that wonderful country of Bangladesh which has such difficult problems to cope with, many of a natural kind. Certainly one of the foremost groups were representatives of the Mennonite Central Committee, fine young Canadians making a most excellent, practical and useful contribution toward the upgrading of agriculture in that country where production from the soil is so important. The views I held a year ago were strengthened by what I saw just a month or two ago.
I think that this is well in place, although there are injustices which my colleagues dealt with last session. Where such relief has been made and such recognition has been extended, I express thanks and extend support and approval.

The minister touched upon and I will not dilate upon the technical amendments, many of which are important and I assume, being an optimist, all of which are helpful.
I am happy we have written in here, as was in Bill C-190, the official function of the Auditor General. He will have plenty to do. There is no doubt about that. The CPP bureaucracy is touching more and more people, and more problems are arising. My own personal contact with Mr. Trudeau and those who are operating the plan has generally been helpful and I appreciate it. However, because of the complexity of the legislation, there are many, many Canadians who are suffering, being misunderstood, being denied and so on.
One of the last references the minister made was to the question of overpayments. There seems to be a measure of relief coming in there. I have always been appalled by any government department which will overpay a citizen and then have the nerve to turn its clutches upon that citizen and say, "We are collecting from you". It has thousands of computers and hundreds of accountants. God help the poor little guy getting a pension or unemployment insurance. It is not his fault that the government makes a mistake. Far from it. With its vast bureaucracy it should not make a mistake, and then draw it out of him month after month after month.
I am sure there is not a member in this House who has not received letters from constituents who have been overpaid. Who overpaid them? It is like the railway mess. Who made it? These people are told that $20 will be deducted from them for the next 10 years, next 40 years or what have you. The poor soul is probably living on something several notches below the poverty line as it is. I say the state has no right to drag out of its citizens mistakes which its own apparatus makes. Far better to correct its own technology than to inflict the cause of its own inefficiency upon the rank and file citizens of this country.
I am happy some effort has been made to make it easier for self-employed persons to enter the plan. For many years it has been an important area of concern. We know that it is relatively easy for the fellow on payroll. He has an accountant or cashier to deduct the exact contribution from him, and so on. However, that very important person who carries on his own business is not a bookkeeper and does not have a bookkeeper. His earnings fluctuate from season to season. He is probably more in need of the cushion which the contributory pension supplies than the man who is on a more permanent basis. For this move I am appreciative. I will support it.
I would like to get back to a question which the minister indicated he and his provincial colleagues have looked at and will look at. That is the question of the place of the housewife, if that is not too old fashioned a word to use- the mother, the head of the home, if that is not too extreme a word to use. I am told it will be difficult, but we have to find equality for the housewife, the housemother, the person who, heaven knows, is importantly employed in our society.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Housespouse.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Housespouse, perhaps that is a good expression. It would be hard for a man with a lisp, but we might be able to take it off.
April 16, 1974

We have to find security for the person who takes on the important role of being the great maintainer of the family unit, which is still basic to our society despite all its changes and apparent changes. It is still the fundamental fabric of the kind of society in which we believe. I believe it is not beyond our ingenuity nor does it exceed our capacity to be able to give to the housewife equality of status.
Suggestions were made in the statement released by the minister. There is an excellent statement by S. June Men-zies, the vice-chairman of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. I think it is very important for these and many other suggestions to be studied as quickly as possible. We do not want someone standing here in 10 years' time telling the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and myself that since it only took 10 years, we should feel proud. We cannot wait 10 years. The group is large, the injustice is vast.
I used to be told that marriage is a partnership. It should not be difficult to extend the concept of partnership to the basic home unit. Someone said that perhaps the best way to do this would be to have the husband pay the wife and pay her premiums. Some might suggest that this is an employer-employee relationship. It just might be a bit dicey, but the partnership I think is a beginning. This must be done quickly. The minister must use his powers of persuasion to convince his provincial counterparts that, as long as this important group is left out, the Canada Pension Plan is a most inadequate umbrella in the realm of provision for our future.
Indeed, I wonder about the whole program. We amend it frequently. Whoever succeeds the minister now sitting opposite us will no doubt introduce further amendments. Suggestions come out of dominion-provincial meetings from time to time. I wonder whether, with all our tailoring, tinkering and re-aligning, we should not be moving toward something more comprehensive. It seems to me we are moving now toward something like a negative income tax or a guaranteed annual income, though I do not think we are admitting it. When I look at the OAS and the CPP, and think of the great need which exists, of the constant tendency to change, the built-in tendency toward complexity, I wonder whether a more serious overview is required than the one to which the minister alluded.
The minister ended as he sometimes does, with an expression of a bursting sense of pride in what had been done. I think a more modest posture would better befit the bill. It is, of course, an improvement, and my hon. colleagues, because we are a highly organized party, will be dealing with various of its aspects. I noticed with some surprise that the minister quickly contradicted the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher) when my hon. friend suggested that inflation was behind the introduction of this measure. Mr. Speaker, because we have indexed payments under this plan there is no way we can sit back and say inflation is out of the picture. That is myopia of the worst kind.
The trouble is that the basic amount is insufficient. The $100 for OAS was insufficient before the act was brought into force. I pointed out that in terms of purchasing power
Canada Pension Plan
recipients were back to 1945. The basic amount is insufficient, and so much per cent of insufficiency does not bring sufficiency, and it certainly does not bring affluence. We are dealing with this matter today because, unfortunately, the government is not able to deal with inflation. Thus, every piece of legislation which can be brought in is being used and, naturally, because some degree of amelioration is afforded, we support these efforts.
However, we do not support the idea that the entire subject is removed from the grievous, groaning and growing problem of inflation in the country. I know it is not. My hon. friends know it is not. And those Canadians, one in four, who live below the poverty line know it is not. The many Canadians who are eking out an existence on OAS or CPP know it is not. So these changes have to be made. It is not because of a technical consideration or the result of an outburst of generosity. It is because too many Canadians are having a hard time.
Mr. Speaker, I have made many mistakes in this House and, I suppose, in life, but one thing I try to avoid is making long speeches. They may never seem as short to others as they appear to me. But if, as a result of this bill some measure of relief is to be brought to thousands of Canadians, there is no disposition on this side to prolong discussion, although it must be noted we are dealing here with a highly complex document and a good deal of questioning will be necessary.
We shall try to restrain our eagerness to get at the football for a few hours because we would not wish to be accused of too hastily passing a measure comprising 46 pages and 57 clauses. It will be taken seriously by the group to which I belong. It will be considered co-operatively, and we expect to see the measure enacted shortly. After that we shall be making suggestions to the minister as to further ways in which he may be able to lighten the burden which has fallen on so many in Canada who are finding the going very tough at the present time.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) in assuring the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) that he should have no difficulty with this bill. We shall be making some comments and suggestions, but it is a bill which we hope will be dealt with expeditiously on second reading, in committee, and at the final stage.
I had the privilege in 1964 and 1965 of being a member of the standing committee which dealt with the original Canada Pension Plan. I do not see many around the House tonight who were members of that committee. However, sitting with us then was a very able and effective private member who has lost that status now he has become a cabinet minister. I refer to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford).
Serving on that committee, one of the things I enjoyed, in addition to the good work I felt the committee did, was the opportunity of getting to know the members of the interdepartmental task force who had put the plan together and who were listening and paying attention to our discussions. I think they did excellent work, and as I have studied the bill now before us, and as I have listened to the

April 16, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
minister tonight, I have felt that whatever task force has succeeded that original one has also done good work.
I understand the concern of the hon. member for Hillsborough when he looks at an amending bill 46 pages long, containing 57 clauses, and says, in his desperation, that it is a complicated piece of legislation. It is true that if you try to read the clauses one by one, and if you wonder where they fit into the original act, it can be a bit confusing; but in the main I wish the Unemployment Insurance Act were as simple as the Canada Pension Plan, and I wish the Income Tax Act were also as simple. There are many sections to the act and many clauses in this amending bill, but in the main I think the Canada Pension Plan is a pretty straight forward piece of legislation.
I think I can say, with the modesty that we all have in this place, that I had something to do in 1964 and 1965 with persuading the Hon. Judy LaMarsh to encourage her colleagues to keep that session going until we got the Canada Pension Plan through. I was a supporter of it then, and I still am. Perhaps what I am doing is establishing my credentials, so that after I have said a few things that will be quite favourable I can offer some suggestions as to the further steps we should take.
I congratulate the minister on the organization of his speech tonight. I thought the way in which he gave us, one by one, the changes that are being made, and then went back and expanded upon some of the more complicated ones, was an excellent way to present the matter to the House. He talked, first of all, of the decision to establish complete equality between male and female contributors to the Canada Pension Plan, and I welcome that most warmly. I deliberately quote the extact words that he used. He said that this amending bill "establishes equality between male and female contributors." This will lead me a little later on to say something about the government's failure to go all the way in establishing equality between male and female Canadians.
At any rate we welcome the changes that are being made in this respect, even if it turns out that the only way that a woman contributor to the Canada Pension Plan achieves equality with a man contributor is either by dying or becoming disabled. There is no equality in terms of the position as between men and women-husband and wife, breadwinner and housewife. There is equality at the point of death or at the point of becoming disabled. Well, that is progress, but let us not take off into paeans of praise as though we have completely solved the problem of equality between the sexes. Even so, Mr. Speaker, we welcome that provision in Bill C-19.
Secondly, the minister dealt with the removal of the employment test that now applies to recipients of the Canada Pension Plan retirement benefit who are between the ages of 65 and 69. This, too, is something that we welcome. Some of us approved of that test ten years ago. I think it is a mark of the way in which society has changed that what seemed acceptable ten years ago is no longer acceptable.
I was glad that the minister made it clear that there is still a voluntary situation between the ages of 65 and 69. A contributor to the Canada Pension Plan is free to retire

any time after the age of 65 and to draw his retirement benefit and earn other money without that affecting the amount of his retirement benefit. He is also free not to take his benefit at that age but to continue working and contributing to the Canada Pension Plan so that later on his retirement benefit is higher. But I think the minister, at any rate by implication, did make it clear that he is not free to do both. A person between the ages of 65 and 69 is not free to take his retirement benefit and continue to work and hope that he can continue to contribute to the Canada Pension Plan; he has to make a choice one way or the other. I am not arguing that such a person should be able to do this, but I hope that the literature that the minister's department will distribute will be very clear on this point.
There is a terrible temptation facing people at that age to collect all the benefits that are coming to them. But bearing in mind that the YMPE is going up each year, and that certain persons might be able to earn a reasonable amount of income during the period when they are between 65 and 69, the advantage of continuing to work and to contribute to the plan, especially in the next little while when the YMPE is going up by rather substantial amounts, might be very great.
Each person will, of course, have to make his own decision; but I hope that the minister will see to it that the information put out is pretty clear. As he said, it can be supplied in a number of ways. Certainly people in receipt of old age security but not yet in receipt of the Canada Pension Plan benefits ought to be provided with the information.
I have the feeling that the material sent out to people who have applied for the old age security pension encourages them a little too strongly to apply for everything there is. The literature encourages them to apply for the guaranteed income supplement whether or not they are entitled to it. It encourages them to apply for the Canada Pension Plan. I simply make the plea that the material that is put out, especially under the new regime, be a little more clear as to the advantages or disadvantages of going one way or the other.
The minister then went on to tell us about the formula for raising the YMPE, the year's maximum pensionable earnings. We welcome very warmly the provisions that have been made in this regard. We were glad last year to approve of the $6,600 level for 1974 and the $7,400 level for 1975, and I think that the formula that has been worked out for succeeding years is a good one.
We welcome also the adjustments that are being made to the YBE, the year's basic exemption. I think the idea of putting it at 10 per cent rather than 12 Vi per cent, especially with the increase in the YMPE, is a good one, particularly for the reason indicated by the minister, namely that this benefits self-employed persons.
The minister then went on to speak of a number of miscellaneous or housekeeping changes that are being made. I found all of them to be good. I am glad the international agreements will be put into effect on a retroactive basis, and I hope that some of the negotiations that are in process with regard to agreements with certain other countries can be expedited. I hope this provision regarding retroactivity will also apply to them as well.
April 16, 1974

Like the hon. member for Hillsborough, I welcome the more humane approach toward overpayments which are the mistake of the administration. I warmly welcome the removal of the four year rule, the rule that required a contributor to check on his records and to make sure that they are up to date, with the restriction that if four years have gone by nothing could be done about any error. I hope there might be some retroactivity with respect to this as well. I know of individual cases where persons are not getting the full benefit to which they feel entitled because there is a dispute over the contributions made on behalf of those persons more than four years ago, and because of the present four year rule nothing can be done about this. As I say, I hope that will be corrected. I welcome the reintroduction of the provision about the payment of legal expenses for persons who are forced by the government side to take a case a step further.
With regard to the provisions for exemption for those who have really established religious scruples, I think we went through this last year and established our position. We had almost got it through; I see no reason that there should be any change and I hope we will not have to kick this around too long this year.
I believe, I can conclude this part of what I want to say by reaffirming my view that the 1973-74 task force, which has done its job, has done as well as the original task force and the changes that are being made in this piece of legislation are good and welcome.
Having said that I should like to comment on some of the issues raised by this bill. First of all I come back to the question of alleged equality between males and females. As the minister said, what this bill establishes is equality between male and female contributors. In other words, just as at present when a male contributor dies he leaves certain survivor benefits to his spouse and children, the legislation now being brought in will confer that same right on the female when she dies, but this is not really the ultimate objective of women's liberation, to get to the point that when a female dies she gets equality with a man.
It seems to me that the basic problem here is that our society, being what it is, has more women not in the work force than there are men not in the work force. There are more housewomen than there are housemen. I know we have a lot of trouble about these terms these days, but I think what I have in mind is clear. There are more female house persons than there are male house persons, and the hon. member who was married only two or three weeks ago, whose interjection is understandable, has not got this all sorted out yet. I extend to him my congratulations in the knowledge that he will learn.
The problem of women, especially those who are not in the work force as defined and yet who work in the home, is that they still, to too large an extent, draw their rights from their men rather than on their own basis. This was the concept in society one hundred or fifty years ago and it has not died yet. I do not ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare in this one bill to solve the whole problem in the concept of marriage, and the whole situation and everything that is involved, but I call upon him-
Canada Pension Plan
perhaps I should put it in other terms by saying I welcome the fact that he realizes there is a problem and is still studying and thinking about it. His paper which he tabled in the committee the other day is evidence of that, and I noted with interest his comment this afternoon when he said he had listened to the debate the other day on the motion of the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman), and noted in particular the suggestion that perhaps a wider use of old age security might be a means of solving the problem in respect of establishing pension equality for men and women.
I see real problems in these schemes for dividing the contributions as between the husband and the housewife. I see real problems in respect of splitting the entitlement that has been earned. That may solve the problem when there is a marriage breakup, but does it really solve the problem of providing pensions for women in their own right in a modern society?
In another context I frequently get into the issue of widows' pensions being 50 per cent, as they are under the Public Service Superannuation Act and under many private pension plans, or even 60 per cent as they are under the pension plan for MPs, but I would simply ask how we ever got into the situation in which a pension is earned by a man or wife as partners, but if the wife dies the husband's pension is 100 per cent for life, whereas if the husband dies his widow's pension is 50 per cent or 60 per cent for life? Where is the equality in that situation? Under the veterans' pensions we have the same kind of situation, the details of which I need not go into, but the concept of 100 or even 300 or 400 years ago, that women's rights stem from their menfold, is still with us, and one of the places where it is very prominent is in this pension area.
I see the problems in respect of permitting housewives to contribute to the plan. If you just do it on the bald basis of letting those who can contribute, of course you provide a bonanza for those who have got money, and you do not do anything for the less wealthy. If you split the contributions for entitlement you create certain problems. Perhaps the hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Macln-nis) has the answer in state salaries for housewives, and let them pay as employed persons. She is not as far out as some people may think. After all, if society has reached the point where it accepts the equality of men and women, let us go all the way.
I must not spend all my time on that phase of the matter, but I wanted to deflate the minister a little with respect to the applause he got from the Liberal benches when he said that we have established absolute equality as between male and female contributors. He is right, that is what he has done, but it is only between male and female contributors. If you are not a contributor you are not in the picture at all, and I say to the minister that he has a long way to go.
I have already complimented the minister on his good work, and I have complimented his task force. I see only two of them within the sound of my voice. At any rate I know this has been worked on by many people, but I think they can keep working on this problem and come up with something. The hon. member for Hillsborough and I expect to be around here for another 10 or 20 years, but

April 16, 1974
Canada Pension Plan
we do not want to wait that long for this problem to be solved.
I now move to another aspect of this matter. I have said that I welcome very warmly the removal of the employment test between the ages of 65 and 69, but the minister need not throw away that employment test, for it was a pretty good one. The thing to do with it now is to apply it between ages 60 and 65. Is that not the next step we should be taking, namely, lowering the pension age under both the Old Age Security Act, and the Canada Pension Plan to age 60 on a voluntary basis? The way you do it on a voluntary basis is by providing that pensions are paid between age 60 and 65 only to those persons who are out of the work force. When I say "out of the work force" I mean either that they got out or were never in it. I add that latter qualification to make sure we are covering the wives at home who never were in the work force.
I think that the minister and his department already have an excellent piece of machinery for this purpose. They are already set up to apply the test of being out of the work force. As I say, I am glad that test is being taken away with respect to those between 65 and 69, but I say: move it over and apply it to those between age 60 and 64, and this will be a real step forward.
I know that the minister is looking at me and saying that every time I speak on pensions I raise the question of pensions at 60. He says to himself: I have tried to tell that fellow that there are other problems in society, and other areas where we have to do things. He knows I agree with him, but I submit that just as I was given that kind of reply when I was trying to get the age brought down from 70 to 65, and eventually we won, we will win this one too. The minister might say: why not bring it down to 48 or 45, or whatever his age is, but we will settle for getting it down to 60 on a voluntary basis.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The change being made with regard to reducing the age for a free pension from 70 to 65 is good, but it does highlight the need to accept the proposition that the pensionable age should be lowered to 60 under both of these major pieces of legislation. I know that there is support for this proposal in all the parties here, and there is just as strong support for it on the government side as there is on this side. I call upon those members over there to make that known to their minister even more strongly than they have been doing.
I was quite interested in what the minister had to say about the new YMPE and the new YBE. This leads to technicalities that I will not go into. I do not want to make it sound any more complicated to the hon. member for Hillsborough than he already thought it was. But I like the

way the minister moved from merely telling us about the changes in YMPE and YBE to the new rates that will develop in a few years' time. He gave some figures which sound pretty good compared with the pension benefits that are being paid today. I want to come back to that in a moment.
I also liked what the minister said when he drew attention to the fact that in some cases this would provide people, if they combined their CPP and their OAS-and even had two OAS payments if it was a man and his wife-with an income equal to about 100 per cent of what they were earning at the time they retired. I say to the minister: bravo, I am delighted that he said it. The notion that somehow or other a pension should be less than what people get when they are working is like the notion about a widow's pension being only 50 or 60 per cent of the husband's pension. It has been around for a long while, but that does not make it right.
What is wrong with the idea that those who have done the work of society for 30 or 40 years should retire, not on a reduced standard of living but on the standard of living that they have helped to make possible? I welcome very strongly the minister's suggestion, even if he put it forward somewhat timidly, that perhaps it is all right to have pensions that in their total amount equal 100 per cent of what a person was earning when he was working. We have come a long way in this parliament of Canada since the day when we had a pension of $20 a month at the age of 70 for those who had nothing else, but we still have a long way to go.
Even if the hon. member for Hillsborough thought that the minister was not as imaginative as he claimed to be, there is at least some imagination here when the minister talks about pension rates that will some day-soon! I hope-enable people to retire and not have to take a reduction in their standard of living. That will be a civilized approach to the problem of retirement, and may we get to it very soon!
I said I was going to come back to the figures the minister quoted for 1980 and 1985. He gave two or three sets of figures, one to do with retirement benefits, one to do with disability benefits, one to do with widows, and so on. Let me say I understood the figures and I recognize that they flow from the new YMPE levels. But the point I wish to make is that the minister was not saying that people who are today drawing CPP benefits will be getting those amounts in 1980 and 1985. What he was saying was that people who retire in 1980 or 1985 and start at that time will get those benefits at those levels. I see that the minister is nodding his head indicating that I am interpreting him correctly. I am concerned about the people who are drawing today's rates. What will be their position in 1980 or 1985?
The minister will probably say to me: did I not remind you about the escalation that takes place which is based on the actual increase in the cost of living? Well, I guess the minister can make my speech for the next five minutes or so-he surely knows what is coming. It still puzzles me that the government should come up with a Canada Pension Plan which is so excellent in its escalation up to the point of retirement. The minister spelled it out tonight. One's pension at the point of retirement is not based on
April 16, 1974

the number of dollars one was making at the age of 18, 25 or 30; it is adjusted by the rise in the wage level, in other words, the rise in the standard of living. That carries through CPP right up to the point of retirement, but come the point of retirement and the poor retired person has to fall back on an index based on the cost of living increase, not on the wage increase.
If we accept the civilized proposition that people at retirement should continue to enjoy the standard of living they have helped to build, I submit that the escalation after retirement, like the escalation of the formula before retirement, should be geared not to the cost of living but to the standard of living.
There are two or three ways in which this can be done. One is to gear it to the wage index; another is to gear it to the gross national product. But to go on for ever leaving it geared to the cost of living index, I submit, is a form of discrimination against those previously retired, and this applies to those who are retired today and it will apply in 1980 to those who will retire in 1978 or 1979.
So I call on the minister to take this part of the whole matter back to the task force, back to his department, and see if they cannot come up with a post retirement escalation formula that is as good as the pre retirement formula. This is not the first time I have proposed this. I argued this at length when we were in the special committee back in 1964 and 1965. In those days we had to settle for a post retirement escalation of only 2 per cent a year. Thank heavens we went beyond that. We now have it on the cost of living and we have it on the actual amount. But, as I have often pointed out, that is not satisfactory because it is always behind. The index one gets in January is based on the increase in August, September and October as compared with the three months previous thereto. It is always behind the price increases that pensioners are having to pay, and, as the hon. member for Hillsborough says, it is an escalation of a base which, to begin with, was too low.
So I say that the last word has not been said in this legislation, regarding escalation. It was good to get it beyond 2 per cent. It is not good enough, however, to leave it where it is. I plead again that the government and the department have in their legislation, in the way they escalate prior to retirement, a basis that they could use advantageously after the time of retirement. So I urge, Mr. Speaker, that escalation after retirement be geared not just to the cost of living but that it be geared to the wage index or the gross national product, so that our people who are members of the Canadian family will be able to enjoy the standard of living that they helped to build, after they retire.
I am coming near the end of what I want to say but I should like to put in another plug about old age security. The minister had a bit to say about the flat rate component and other benefits. I understand the thinking there, but is it not a fact that as time goes on the old age security in more and more cases becomes a flat rate component in the pensioner's total benefit? Just as a disabled person gets a flat rate plus a certain percentage so the average
Canada Pension Plan
retired person will have an old age security flat rate payment and the Canada Pension payment on top.
I want to make again the argument that we move more in the direction of equality and fairness if we keep on raising what I now call the flat rate component, in other words, keep on raising old age security. I noticed that when the minister gave his figures about what pensions would be in the future he included old age security. He left the door open for larger amounts. You just do not assume that old age security will stay at $100. I can tell him it had better not stay there.

speechtext:
The minister says it is not there now. True, it has gone up now to $110.09 per month but the difficulty is just that bit of lethargy that the minister revealed right there. It has not stayed at $100, it has gone up and he does not have to do anything! It could go up every three months, but not by the kind of amount that is necessary to put our retired people in the position where they are enjoying a standard of living that they helped get. I think substantial increases are still called for in the basic amount of the old age pension. It is a method to follow so far as wives are concerned, but it is also a method to follow so far as fairness across the board is concerned.
When the minister made it clear that he was making a rather full speech tonight I had thought that he would deal with some of the newspaper editorial attacks that have been made recently on the Canada Pension Plan. I was looking forward to that. After it was all over I decided I was just as glad that he did not pay any attention to them. Maybe I should do the same, but I will take a moment or two to say that most of those attacks on programs like the Canada Pension Plan, old age security or transfer payments, come from persons or editorial writers or interests that just do not like the concept of equality.
I know it is true that as pensions go up they play their part in inflation and they play their part in rising costs, so that $110.09 per month is not worth as much as $100 a month was six months ago. But to the extent that we put more payments that are based on equality in the hands or pockets of our people, we build a more just, a more human and a more decent society.
It is in the area of family allowances where we have universal payments, it is in the area of our people aged 65 and over where we have universal old age security, that we come closest in my view to establishing social justice. I think this can be pursued still further by a substantial increase in the basic old age pension, say up to $200 a month this year, and by further improvements that are still in prospect with respect to the Canada Pension Plan.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude by saying two things that may sound opposite but are both true. I am excited, I am proud of what I have seen accomplished in the parliament of Canada in the last several decades in the pension field. I well remember what it was when I came here-$20 a month at age 70 with a means test and no family allowance. We have come a long way. It is good; it is exciting; Canada can be proud of what we have done. But we still
