subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RELIGIOUS SECTS, EARNINGS FORMULA, BASIC EXEMPTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you very much for this opportunity to join in the debate. We have had a very eloquent and clear exposition by the minister who went into the broad aspects and details, and this is a grand bill. We had the short and excellent presentation of the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) and this final, shall we say, almost peroration by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I think the minister will be glad to have had his agenda looked after by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for the next two to five years.
We all have to have something to say, even though it might be trite when following the previous speakers. I should like to remind the House that this bill is really an act to amend the Canada Pension Plan, and it continues the government's policy to bring in legislation which aims to improve the lot of the old people and which will really equalize benefits in our society. It now includes women generally but, as has been said by other speakers, we hope it will eventually include the non-paid housewife or, in some cases, the non-paid house spouse.
The bill includes the provisions of Bill C-190 which died prematurely when parliament rose last summer, but which was an acceptable interim development in the evolution of the Canada Pension Plan. The bill also provides more changes of a technical nature. These have been well discussed and are evidence of needed change, and they will prevent inconveniences or even unfairness to the pensioner.
Before dealing with explicit changes I should like to remind the House that the government believes in federal-provincial conferences-in other words, communication. These are becoming more frequent and more successful. It is really a "must" in order fully to integrate regions with the central parliament. In fact it is to be hoped that in time the misunderstanding and hostility of areas, provinces or regions, either among themselves or directed toward the federal government, will greatly lessen as communication becomes more effective. I say that without being partisan.
Be that as it may, the Edmonton meeting of February 19 and 20 this year was most satisfactory. The health and welfare ministers wished to continue to emphasize the review of social security which had been begun in the previous year. They all agreed that we should assist the poor and disadvantaged, including the unemployed and the underpaid. They reaffirmed their agreed-on principle to help people provide for their retirement, for sickness, accident and unemployment. Of course, they included income support, where required. Because a guaranteed annual income or an omnibus program to replace all existing programs did not appear desirable at once, and there are many reasons for this, they delegated their officials to continue discussing this matter; but they themselves proceeded to the practical questions of the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans.

One of the priority issues was equal treatment of male and female contributors, and the other concerned how a housewife or spouse remaining at home could contribute to these plans. The present bill has actually been based on the amendments which this meeting at Edmonton thought necessary. So, we already have, as it were, a national consensus on its provisions.
Some worry was expressed today about our ability to pay for these plans. Speaking on the bill previously before the House, the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie), whom I respect, was worried in case the Old Age Security and Canada Pension Plan would tend to reduce the need for savings. Such a suggestion is not really correct. I think it has been demonstrated that there was greater saving per capita from income in the last year or so than at any other time in our history.
Some members are also worried in case this bill will add to inflationary pressures. I think inflation is with us, and must be faced and accepted. We should realize that Canada cannot take a stance alone. The only stance that we would take should be one that recognizes that Canada is in one of the best positions among the countries of the world, can afford such plans, and should undertake them. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in what he said about equality. There is no equality when some people can hardly get along on what they have while others have immense wealth. I think there must be some kind of income redistribution, and the Canada Pension Plan helps in this.
To make members happier let me refer them to a recent edition of the Wall Street Journal. We should all read it. It forecasts that Canada's future, despite inflation, will probably be that of leader of all developed countries. We are almost in that position now. We will be there 30 years from now. I believe that we can well afford any plan we can bring in to equalize incomes, particularly of the aged, and to make more equal the status of women in our society.
The status of women generally, their acceptance in the labour force, and the need for equality of treatment for women in the matter of pensions and legal rights: are things that have all received a great deal of public attention. Separated or divorced women, and children of failed marriages all require new provisions in our system of justice. This bill, in so far as it is now possible for us to move in this direction, faces up to these problems. It is axiomatic that we, as a parliament, will have to update constantly our legislation as society continues to evolve.
As we become aware of new attitudes to the position of women in society and in the home, we must adjust our pension schemes accordingly. We now question any different treatment of women as contributors to and beneficiaries of the Canada Pension Plan. In addition, we wonder why housewives at home cannot participate. The first concern is being looked after in this legislation, Bill C-19, the second issue will continue to be studied, because implementing it is difficult and complex. These things must be discussed by the public at large as well as by governments.
Originally, the Canada Pension plan was conceived as being part of the income maintenance system and as involving both public and private sectors. Early on most
April 16, 1974

people thought that the old Age Security Plan would look after retired people, as it applied to wage earners and non wage earners alike. Therefore this evening I am appreciative of the fact that I have an opportunity to participate in this debate on Bill C-19 in order to express some views with regard to this very important measure.
As my colleague, the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), pointed out, this is a very difficult and complex bill. It is extensive and complicated. There is a great deal of detailed work in connection with it.
It is difficult enough to try and plough through the provisions of the bill. It is also very difficult to analyse the contribution which the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) made when he introduced this measure today. He introduced a great many features that possibly have precluded our study thus far. In addition, he placed a great deal of statistical data before us. I am sure hon. members will agree it will be absolutely impossible to assess it all and put it in proper perspective in the short time that has elapsed since the minister presented the measure.
The preamble to the Canada Pension Plan Booklet (1970) by the then Minister of National Health and Welfare, the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), states:
The Canada Pension plan, inaugurated in 1966, is a contributory social security program designed to provide a basic level of protection against the contingencies of retirement, disability and death.
There has been a considerable degree of discussion, even thus far in the debate, regarding the various levels of income and the inequality of income as far as Canadians are concerned. It is tragic that in a society like ours, with our vast resources, there are still many people living below the poverty line while others are living on a much higher level. We can apply the same terminology that is used in international affairs when talking about the have and have-not nations. We can talk about the have and have-not people of this country. Anything that is done in an endeavour to remove the great disparities that exist, especially any attempt to bring the income of every Canadian up to a suitable level, should certainly receive the support of every member of this House.
I referred to the statement of the former Minister of National Health and Welfare. I suggest that was a noble

resolve, a noble step at the time of its-inception. I am sure that every member of parliament at that time, including myself, realized that it was not to be considered in any way as the total and complete answer to the needs of Canadians at that time, much less in the future.
It was understandable that, besides the inadequacies and injustices obvious at that time, there would be others that might only be discernible as the plan got under way. Because of that fact, it is not surprising that we are again being called upon to consider additional proposals designed to make the plan more responsive to the needs of society today.
This may not be the most auspicious time to consider the confrontation presently taking place between the "work ethic" advocate versus the "welfare" apostle, but suffice it to say this bill is predicated on the principle that an individual desires and is required to engage in constructive and remunerative employment to provide for his or her own needs and the needs of those who are dependent upon him or her, as the case may be. The great preponderance of Canadians have enough pride and character to pay their own way if opportunity is given them and government keep their hands from getting too deep in the taxpayer's pocket.
One of the most obvious problems at the present time is that through mismanagement on the part of the government, and its evident inability to control inflationary pressures, even the hardest working and most conscientious citizens of this nation are penalized, and the more thrifty they are, the more they are gouged by the tax collector. In many respects this government is undermining and discouraging the will of Canadians to work and save by implementing unfair and iniquitous tax policies.

subtopic: COMMUNICATIONS-CABLEVISION-REQUEST FOR EARLY APPROVAL OF APPLICATIONS TO IMPROVE RECEPTION IN MANITOBA
COMMUNICATIONS-CABLEVISION-REQUEST FOR EARLY APPROVAL OF APPLICATIONS TO IMPROVE RECEPTION IN MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) is in the House this evening. On March 28 I asked the minister a question respecting an application before the CRTC which would allow for the moving of antennae presently being used for cablevision reception in the Winnipeg area, replacing them in an area in southeastern Manitoba, and then utilizing microwave signals.
I should like to point out that this application was made on behalf of various Winnipeg cablevision companies as far back as June, 1973. Recently the Chairman of the CRTC has been making pronouncements regarding Canadian content on CBC programs. I should like to tell the minister that there are a number of areas in Manitoba, not in remote regions but within 60 or 70 miles of Winnipeg, which at present are getting only a minimum of CBC coverage, and no alternate coverage whatever.
The CBC sat on this application of June, 1973, and did not hear it until February 7, 1974, some eight months later. To add to the delay the commission then deferred its decision until May 14. I want to impress upon the minister that if we are to have the benefit of an alternate service in parts of Manitoba other than the Winnipeg area, a microwave system must be approved.
In his reply to me on March 28 the minister said the CRTC was doing its best and that the government did not make decisions for the commission. Yet the CRTC is an agent of government and has a responsibility to the public to express its views, whether for or against an application.
Letters of intent have been issued to the CRTC by people in the Pine Falls area asking that cable television be extended in that area. But according to the workings of the CRTC, the commission must first advertise that it is willing to receive applications. However, it refuses to do this. So the people in Pine Falls are deprived even of an opportunity to present an application for cable television, and to see their application either accepted or rejected. Surely the least the people of the area can expect is that they will be heard. I quote from a letter written by a constituent in that area:
I have made a start on a brief to present at the May 14 hearings but am not going to do any more work on it until such time as I know definitely I shall be allowed to present it. Operating in its usual fashion, the CRTC has not yet seen fit to acknowledge our request which was mailed on March 22.
All we are asking is, first, that an application having been made we can expect a decision after eight months. Second, we are asking that Canadians be heard. We question the position of the commission that applications cannot be received until advertisements have been published to that effect. The CRTC is an arm of the Department of Communications. Applications should be heard and decided, for or against, on their own merits and not be deferred, or left unheard, because the commission has some bureaucratic reason for declining to take action. It is incumbent on the minister to demand of the CRTC that it at least give the Canadian people their democratic rights-
April 16, 1974

that it should hear applications and then decide whether or not to approve them.

subtopic: COMMUNICATIONS-CABLEVISION-REQUEST FOR EARLY APPROVAL OF APPLICATIONS TO IMPROVE RECEPTION IN MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first like to say that I do not agree with the hon. member that the CRTC is an arm of the Department of Communications. It is a quasi judicial body, and that creates an entirely different situation, as I am sure he will agree. The delays the hon. member has been pointing out are real. I think his facts are correct. I should like to inform him, though, that they are not of a bureaucratic nature.
The delay in holding the Manitoba hearing in Winnipeg arose primarily from the position taken by the government of Manitoba, which had publicly advised all broadcasters and cable television licencees in Manitoba that its department of communications was working on a telecommunications position paper for Manitoba. This announcement was made publicly on November 15, 1972, and the position paper was tentatively scheduled for completion by midsummer, 1973. Since the federal agencies are generally, rightly or wrongly, criticized for not consulting with the provinces or for not taking into account the wishes and needs of the provinces, the CRTC thought it wise to wait for this document, which although it had been announced would be completed by the summer of 1973 has not yet been completed.
So this is the reason for the delay. The CRTC could not delay any further. I do not know whether the Manitoba white paper was the great design that the provincial government wanted to put out, and that it will be out by May 14. I do not have the faintest notion, and I suspect the CRTC has not either. Surely the CRTC itself would provide the hon. member with the decision to which he is alluding after the May 14 Winnipeg public hearing. It is not only one or two isolated decisions that are at stake here but the whole planning and development of telecommunications and a cable system for the province of Manitoba.
Here are the facts. I understand the concerns of the hon. member and I share them. I can assure him the CRTC shares them also, and that after the May hearing the procrastination will come to an end and a decision will be taken.

subtopic: HEALTH-INCIDENCE OF SILICOSIS AMONG URANIUM WORKERS-ACTION BY MINISTER OF LABOUR
HEALTH-INCIDENCE OF SILICOSIS AMONG URANIUM WORKERS-ACTION BY MINISTER OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over a week ago I raised the issue of health safety in the uranium mines at Elliot Lake in northern Ontario. For the benefit of those members of the House who are not aware of the background of this particular mining operation a quick sketch is essential.
Uranium mining and milling came into being in Elliot Lake in 1955. The ore is contained in a base, 70 per cent of which is free silica as compared with 4 per cent to 8 per cent in the Sudbury camp. It was readily recognized that mining the Elliot Lake ore body presented a very significant potential risk, but it was believed that the existing mining technology was adequate to cope with this problem. No doubt, Mr. Speaker, whatever second thoughts
Adjournment Debate
there were quickly evaporated in the face of the enormous and dazzling contracts secured by the federal government from the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission through its own agency, the Eldorado Mining and Refining Company, contracts worth a total value of $1.5 billion.
Unfortunately, specific delivery dates were set down and deliveries were required to be completed by 1963. Also, under risk of cancellation, these deliveries were to commence on specific dates. What followed was an accelerated exploitation of the ore body in order for the mining companies to honour their commitments. This involved high wages, with particularly high bonus incentives, round the clock mining, short cuts, and always at their backs the threat of contract cancellation.
In this highly charged atmosphere of big profit, dust control and other measures of health safety assumed roles of secondary importance. Inevitably, as always in a community solely dependent upon the mining industry, the bust occurred in the 1960s when the options for contract renewal by the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission were not taken up after 1959. Then in the late sixties, and particularly between 1970 and the end of 1972, a pattern began to emerge. Dust effects-the various X-ray stages leading to silicosis-began appearing in miners with little or no previous mining experience before Elliot Lake. The present situation at Elliot Lake is that some 10 per cent of the work force have pulmonary disabilities ranging up to 40 per cent.
As far back as 1972 the United Steelworkers of America, which represents the miners in Elliot Lake, was in contact with the then Minister of Labour, Mr. Martin O'Connell, requesting his intervention on behalf of the miners' health and safety in the uranium mines. Indeed, in a letter to Mr. Paul Falkowski of USWA District 6, Mr. O'Connell admitted that the uranium mines of Canada are subject to federal jurisdiction. In the same letter the minister stated that employment safety and health in the uranium mines are subject to the provisions of the Atomic Energy Control Act, administered by the Atomic Energy Control Board.
Because of the persistence of the steelworkers union, the Ontario department of natural resources carried out an environment quality survey in the uranium mines at Elliot Lake. The workers involved have been seriously critical of several aspects of this survey. One such criticism is that the instruments used were not modern enough to be capable of producing accurate and satisfactory results.
In addition, criticism has been raised to the effect that normal operating conditions were altered deliberately to such a degree as to produce absolutely false results. Furthermore, any activities which are responsible for increasing or producing dust concentration in the mine ceased a number of hours before the "so-called" environmental survey started and samples of the mine air were collected. Crushers were shut down and normally dusty areas were washed down prior to the investigation of the mine environment.
This survey ended up as a whitewash for Mr. Stephen B. Roman, owner of Denison Mines and Rio Algoma. It was because of this obvious "dodge the ball" game being

April 16, 1974
Adjournment Debate
played by the provincial Tory government with its corporate friends in the mining sector that the United Steelworkers of America once again approached the federal government.
Uranium mines of Canada are within the federal jurisdiction. Furthermore, I hold here a document numbered P.C. 1972-431, dated March 7, 1972 entitled "Regulations Respecting the Use, Handling and Storage of Dangerous Substances and Radiation Emitting Devices in Federal Works, Undertakings and Businesses". In Clause 2 entitled "Interpretation", "Minister" means the Minister of Labour, and "Division Chief" means the Chief, Accident Prevention Division, Accident Prevention and Compensation Branch, Department of Labour, Ottawa.
In addition, Clause 10 states specifically, and I quote in part:
Subject to Section 11, every employer shall ensure that the concentration of any dangerous substance that may be carried by the air in any area where an employee is working
(a)	does not exceed the threshold limit value recommended by the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists in its pamphlet "Threshold Limit Values for Air Borne Contaminants 1971" as amended from to time, or
(b)	conforms with any standard that follows good industrial safety practice, and is acceptable to the division chief.
Clause 13 amplifies this, and I quote in part again:
Where the atomosphere of any area in which an employee is working is subject to contamination by a dangerous substance, the employer shall ensure that the atmosphere is sampled and tested as frequently as
(a)	may be necessary to ensure that the level of contamination does not at any time exceed the safe limits prescribed by Section 10, 11 and 12, or
(b)	is directed in writing by the regional safety officer.
When I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) to assume his responsibilities to the uranium miners of Elliot Lake, he said:
It is not within my jurisdiction... the jurisdiction falls under the Atomic Energy Control Board and certain activities are undertaken by the Radiation Division of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
My colleague, the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Nesdoly), raised the issue with the Atomic Energy Control Board when that board appeared before the House's Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works. What was the outcome? The Atomic Energy Control Board neatly passed the buck to the provincial government. The Elliot Lake miners in trying to avoid the "dodge the ball game" of the Ontario Tory government, have come face to face with the federal Liberal government's game of passing the buck.
The use of uranium as a source of energy is becoming more widespread and its mining will become more extensive. It is absolutely imperative, in view of the urgent and grave nature of the health risk, that the government ensure that the proper testing is done to determine and establish safe working conditions for the uranium miners of Elliot Lake and Canada. I hope that the minister, or his parliamentary secretary, will not stand up here tonight and tell me again that this is not within his jurisdiction. The responsibility is being passed from hand to hand, and no adequate action is being taken. The federal Minister of Labour is ultimately and morally responsible for what is happening to those workers in the uranium mines.

The problems have been identified and pointed out by the workers themselves, the United Stellworkers of America and the Workmen's Compensation Board of Ontario. I, as a member of this House, am asking that the minister step in on behalf of those workers and make damn sure that their health is protected. If that involves stepping on the toes of the Atomic Energy Control Board, or Stephen P. Roman, then I suggest the minister get his walking shoes on right now. Thank you, companeros.

subtopic: HEALTH-INCIDENCE OF SILICOSIS AMONG URANIUM WORKERS-ACTION BY MINISTER OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject of the uranium mining industry and Part IV of the Canada Labour Code (Safety of Employees) falls under the following headings: First, the general responsibility for occupational health and safety in the uranium industry. The application of Part IV of the Canada Labour Code (Safety of Employees) is by virtue of Section 80 "subject to any other act of the Parliament of Canada and any regulations thereunder-". The Atomic Energy Control Act therefore takes precedence over Part IV of the Canada Labour Code and regulations thereunder.
The second heading is the role and responsibility of the Atomic Energy Control Board. Under the Atomic Energy Control Act, the Atomic Energy Control Board is generally responsible for all matters pertaining to the occupational health and safety of employees of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited and Eldorado Nuclear Limited, including the uranium mines in Saskatchewan and Ontario.
Third, the role of the Canada Department of Labour respecting uranium mining. The Department of Labour has no statutory responsibility for occupational health and safety related to the mining or processing of uranium. It has nervertheless expressed its general interest in the subject to the chairman of the Atomic Energy Control Board and offered any assistance it could provide. These matters continue to be handled by the board in accordance with its regular policies and procedures.
Fourth, delegation of responsibility to provincial governments. The Atomic Energy Control Board has delegated responsibility in the operational safety and health fields to the two provinces by arrangement. It is understood that the board does not routinely receive reports concerning occupational safety and accident prevention inspections and surveys from the provincial agencies.
With regard to Ontario, under the delegated authority inspections are performed by the Ontario ministry of natural resources for any mine which is subject to the Ontario mining act. The Ontario ministry of health carries out inspections upon request of the Ontario ministry of natural resources. There does not appear to be any established program of regular monitoring of health conditions in the uranium mine.
With regard to Saskatchewan, the mines inspection branch of the Saskatchewan department of labour-formerly under the mineral resources department-has carried out regular annual inspections of the Beaver Lodge mine. The Saskatchewan department of health formerly performed annual inspection, but this is not known to have been done for at least the past five years.

subtopic: COMMEMORATION-INQUIRY AS TO POSSIBILITY OF EVENTS TO HONOUR MACKENZIE KING, ARTHUR MEIGHEN AND J. S. WOODSWORTH
COMMEMORATION-INQUIRY AS TO POSSIBILITY OF EVENTS TO HONOUR MACKENZIE KING, ARTHUR MEIGHEN AND J. S. WOODSWORTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on more than one occasion in this chamber and in other assemblies of people I have deplored our nation's seeming reluctance to pay adequate tribute and give sufficient praise to the men and women of an earlier date who contributed so mightily and worthily to Canada's greatness.
I have felt this lack in our timidity about commemorating the birth dates of our founding fathers. We are also most timid and neglectful when it comes to commemorative stamps. It took us more than a century to place the likenesses of former prime ministers on the paper currency of the realm.
I thought the coincidence of three distinguished Canadian political leaders sharing the same year of birth, 1874, sufficiently significant to raise the matter in the oral question period. I refer to the Rignt Hon. Arthur Meighen, Reverend James Shaver Woodsworth and the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King in that order to indicate one thing, their order of birth in the year 1874, one century ago.
Mr. Meighen, born in Anderson, Ontario, on June 16, 1874, was a brilliant scholar, able lawyer, successful businessman and an outstanding expert on Shakespeare. But he was superb as a parliamentarian. It is doubtful that this historic chamber or its physical predecessor ever heard a greater debater. He was first elected to the House of Commons in 1908. He went on to serve in major minister-ies in the Borden government, and in 1920 became prime minister at 46, the youngest in the nation's history.
Brilliant though his career was, he was singularly unfortunate in his efforts to lead his party to electoral victories. His great skills were not of themselves sufficient for the
Adjournment Debate
times and the circumstances. His biographer, Roger Graham, refers to Meighen's delusion that in politics the weight of evidence and the force of argument determine the issue.
In Mr. Woodsworth Canadian public life had a major contributor to the social consciousness reflected in parliamentary action and debate. A dedicated champion of the underdog, this great visionary saw some of his visions become reality as the lot of rank and file Canadians was gradually bettered through a developing awareness that the institution of government should help most those who most needed help. While in this House from 1921 to 1942 he was always with a minor party, if with a party at all. But no one would designate as minor his impact upon the House and his contribution to the improvement of the life and standards of the Canadian people.
Mr. King, under whose prime ministership I lived part of my youth, was also a social reformer but more notably a political performer. Like Macdonald and Laurier, he knew the positive and dynamic value of compromise, and his ability in winning elections has made his name a leading one in the roster of successful political leaders. A matchless sense of timing, a capacity for patience, a keen ability for judging men-these were but some of the ingredients of his mastery of the political arts.
Three men so different, yet men of rare distinction, men who would be deserving of special note in any free parliament. These three-Meighen, Woodsworth, and King-are uniquely ours. Canada's parliament and Canada's people should find a fitting way to honour this illustrious trio in this, the centennial of their birth.
